courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Introduction to Human Health
courses.description: Introduces students to the study of human health through the lens of anthropology, where we examine health not just as a biological state, but as a product of evolution, culture, society, and environment. Designed for students across the university who are interested in health, including pre-med, pre-public health, and anthropology majors/minors.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Introductory Cultural Anthropology
courses.description: The nature of culture: survey of the range of cultural phenomena, including material culture, social organization, religion, and other topics.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: World Archaeology
courses.description: An introduction to archaeology and the history of humankind from the earliest times through the advent of literate civilization and cities, also processes of cultural change and the importance of archaeology to people and societies today. Partly self-paced learning.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Introduction to Archaeology
courses.description: Introduction to archaeology and the prehistory of humankind from the earliest times up to the advent of civilization and cities, also processes of cultural change.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Introductory Biological Anthropology
courses.description: An introductory course in human evolutionary biology. Natural selection and its genetic basis are used to highlight a variety of human traits. The fossil record is addressed, but the course takes more of an adaptationist than a paleontological perspective.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Introductory Biosocial Anthropology
courses.description: An introduction to our evolved, universal human nature, the evolution of the human mind, and how they shape behavior, social life, and culture. Topics include friendship, mate choice, incest avoidance, cooperation, revenge, status, jealousy, emotions, group formation, and intergroup aggression.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Health Beyond Borders
courses.description: Investigates global health through the integrated lenses of biological anthropology, cultural anthropology, and bioarchaeology, moving across deep time and the contemporary world to ask what it means to be healthy, sick, and cared for across human societies. Themes include: the ecology of emerging infectious disease, the politics of medicine, the comparative organization of healthcare systems, indigenous health sovereignty, and the challenge of chronic illness in an aging world.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Methods in the Human Behavioral Sciences
courses.description: Introduces the design and analysis of scientific studies on human behavior. Emphasizes theory-based testing of hypotheses, with examples drawn from human ecology, physiology, and behavior. Covers a range of quantitative and qualitative methods including observation, surveys, and experiments.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Violence and the Japanese State
courses.comments: History 25, Japanese 25, and Anthropology 25 are the same course.
courses.description: Examines historiographically and sociologically the Japanese State's various engagements in violent acts during war and peace times.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Independent Studies
courses.comments: Students must have a 3.0 overall GPA. May be taken for a maximum of four units of Anthropology 99 per quarter, and can be repeated for a maximum of 8 units. Students are limited to five units per quarter and 30 units total in all 98/99/198/199/199AA-ZZ courses combined.
courses.description: Introduction to research in Anthropology. Independent research under the guidance of a faculty member in the department. Course offers exceptional students the opportunity to undertake independent research or work in a research group.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Basic Archaeological Concepts
courses.description: A survey of important archaeological methods of excavation, analysis, and interpretation. Focus will be on the problems and promise of various approaches to the explanation of past human behavior.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Activist Anthropology
courses.description: Activist scholarship seeks to combine rigorous research and political commitment to achieve empirical and theoretical understanding of social processes. While open access to information has democratized knowledge production, academic work is still necessary to ask the questions and find the answers to address social injustice and inequality. In this course, we explore the methods and results of more than two decades of activist research.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Human-Wildlife Interactions
courses.description: Survey of human-wildlife interactions (e.g., bushmeat, pet trade, crop-raiding). Students examine cascading effects on wildlife, landscapes, and human populations, as well as mitigating approaches relating to our changing perceptions of wildlife and nature.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Anthropology of Health
courses.comments: ANTH Majors and ANTH Minors must take this course for letter grade to apply to their Upper Division ANTH Major Requirements.
courses.description: We often think of health as a biological process. And while biological processes are certainly central to health outcomes, these processes are influenced by many things, including human evolutionary history and the environment(s) and culture(s) around us. Explores ways that biology and culture impact human health, across the life course and across cultures. Students gain important background knowledge on diet and nutrition, growth, reproductive health, aging, and infectious disease from a global perspective and will walk away with an understanding of impactful social and environmental determinants of health disparities.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Biology of Women
courses.comments: ANTH 105BW was formerly known as ANTH197BW.
courses.description: An exploration of female and womxn’s reproductive lives from an evolutionary and biocultural perspective. We will focus on physiological, ecological, and social aspects of womxn’s development across cultures from before birth, through reproductive processes like pregnancy, birth, lactation, menopause, and aging. Examples will be drawn from contemporary human societies, including many small-scale societies, although non-human primates will also be considered occasionally. This class will include lectures, discussion in multiple formats, and other modes of learning.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Cultural Evolution
courses.prereq_text: Upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
courses.description: This course takes a scientific and evolutionary lens to cultural phenomena. We will consider the origins of culture in non- humans and humans, and how tendencies to imitate, conform, teach and uphold social norms via punishment and reward shape behavioral variation.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Educating the Native
courses.description: We look at different educational projects, such as Indian boarding Schools, English-only laws, the "indirect rule" of the British colonies. We address the not-always-clear line between education as a form of social control or as a form of liberation.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Human Universals
courses.description: A critical overview of those characteristics of human psyche, behavior, society, and culture that are allegedly found among all peoples: the constants of human nature.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: The Anthropology of Food
courses.description: Critical survey of different anthropological approaches to food production and consumption. Topics may include relations between agricultural forms and political systems; the meanings of feasting; cooking; class, race, and gender; food and national identity; food sovereignty, food justice and more.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Indigenous People and the Nation State in the Americas
courses.comments: CH ST 109 and ANTH 113 are the same course.
courses.description: The changing relationship between indigenous people and the state. Compare the differences and similarities between indigenous peoples' mobilizations in the cases of Canada, USA, Ecuador, Chile, Guatemala, Bolivia and Mexico.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Structuralism and Structural Functionalism
courses.description: Outlines a segment of the history of anthropological theory through the 20th century ethnological traditions of structuralism and structural functionalism. Foregrounds select anthropologists who have contributed to these traditions, including Emile Durkheim, E.E. Evans-Pritchard and Eduardo Viveros de Castro; their critics: Judith Butler, Saba Mahmood, and Marilyn Strathern. The goal of the course is to organize the discursive structure around which these thinkers cohere and to question the place of these traditions in contemporary anthropology. Topics of interest include institutions/agency; nature/culture; subsistence, desire, and need; language and semiotics; magic/religion; gender/sexuality; and ontology/metaphysics.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Language, Culture, and Place
courses.description: Focuses on the dialectical interplay between humans and the environment and how people use language to classify, make sense of, and attribute moral and symbolic meaning to places and landscapes.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Myth, Ritual and Symbol
courses.description: Uses ethnographic case studies, films and performance videos to explore myth, ritual, and symbolism cross-culturally. Compares and contrasts the symbolic dimensions of gender and ethnic identity, world view, social and political organization and change in different societies.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Borders and Borderlands
courses.description: The theoretical concept of "borderlands" examined through a discussion of the societies, economics and cultures that form on geopolitical borders. The Mexico-U.S. border will be discussed in detail.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Anthropology of Love and Friendship
courses.description: Examines love and friendship as central anthropological and political concerns. Drawing on a broad range of ethnographic work, explores how intimacy, attachment, care, and obligation are shaped by kin relations, gender, sexuality, race, class, citizenship, and political economy. Emphasizing lived and embodied experience, the course examines how love and friendship are felt, cultivated, regulated, and contested. We also consider how affective ties generate ethical claims, social belonging, and possibilities for solidarity, refusal, and alternative forms of living.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Ethnography as Care
courses.description: Traditionally, ethnography was conceived as the objective study of exotic Others. In this course, we will survey feminist ethnographic debates that approach ethnography as emotional labor that has never been value-neutral, but rather “partial” in the sense of incomplete and interested (Haraway 1988). We will also approach ethnographic research as embedded in broader “affective economies” (Ahmed 2004) that include humanitarianism, colonialism, development, and human rights. By centering ethnography as a “matter of care” (Puig de la Bella Casa 2017), we will ask questions such as how and why we are affectively drawn to our research and how we practice ethnography with an eye towards ethnographic accountability.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: The Anthropology of Resistance
courses.description: Examines resistance, refusal, protest, and dissent as central objects of anthropological inquiry, attending to the everyday, collective, and affective dimensions of political action. Drawing on ethnographic work across diverse contexts and historical periods, we explore how resistance takes shape through protest, refusal, sabotage, care, coalitional survival, and alternative forms of sociality.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Psychological and Phenomenological Anthropology
courses.description: Examines a subfield of anthropology whose conceptual frameworks rely on traditions of phenomenology, psychoanalysis, and psychology. The course focuses on the emergence of this subfield, its texts and discourses, and its importance for anthropological inquiry. It also explores the themes it foregrounds, including medicine, the body, the imagination, existence, therapeutic worlds, addiction, gender and sexuality, religious traditions, shamanism, and colonialism. Throughout our readings we also consider the deep affinities between anthropology, phenomenology, and psychoanalysis, how they have historically intersected, and their relevance for contemporary anthropological analysis.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Genetics, Natural Selection, and Human Evolution
courses.description: An introduction to the nature and role of genes in evolution, in natural selection, in sexual reproduction, in cellular regulation, in human development, in structuring universal human adaptive design, and in creating individual and intergroup similarities and differences.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Anthropology of Security
courses.description: Examines the infrastructures, practices, and concepts that emerge from securitization. Critically analyzes how security becomes entangled with the state as a legal, political, and social form and how securitization marks a new mode of power and governance irreducible to the demands of sovereignty. Topics include the relationship between freedom, rights, and protection; surveillance and its technologies; material and immaterial violence; global networks and the international; force and coercion; policing and law enforcement; and the politics of borderlands and migration.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Feeding Ecology of Primates and Humans
courses.description: Foraging and feeding patterns in primates with some discussion of human patterns. Topics include digestive physiology; measurement of energy flows and food availability; foraging theory; and the evolutionary context of human diets.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Data Analysis for the Social Sciences with R
courses.description: An introduction to the scientific process and data analysis using the programming language R. Students harness fundamentals of data manipulation, visualization, and research workflows to refine and present hypotheses and results on social science datasets. Introduces modeling methods.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Capitalism
courses.comments: Recommend taking ANTH 2 prior, but not necessary.
courses.description: This course presents the contribution of Marxist analysis to anthropology. Among the topics explored are: the commodity; accumulation; reproduction; class; peasants and capital; land and labor; hegemony.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Anthropology of Gender
courses.description: The cross-cultural study of gender from a feminist perspective. Topics may include gender, race, and class; gender and nature; gender and the division of labor; gender and kinship; gender and subjectivity; gender and sexuality; gender and the state; gender and knowledge/discourse.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Laboratory Methods and Biomarkers for the Social Sciences
courses.comments: Course Materials Fee Charged.
courses.description: This course spans a broad range of theory and methods involved in using biomarkers in the social sciences. Theory comes from areas of behavioral research including, behavioral endocrinology, behavioral ecology, evolutionary medicine, and public health. Methods focus on but are not limited to biomarker sampling (saliva, urine, feces, blood), quality controls and processing, and the principles of immunoassays used to measure biomarker concentrations.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Anthropology of Racial Slavery
courses.description: Examines the world-building and world-destroying structures produced from the transatlantic slave trade. While the primary focus is the formation of slavery in the United States, readings will also consider the place of Africa and Latin America in relation to the transatlantic slave trade. Fundamentally, the course introduces students to the numerous mechanisms used to maintain the being of the slave as slave through the law, political economy, criminal justice, and in the organization of political and social life. We will pay attention to the encounters slavery made possible between intersecting worlds and the concepts that underly this relationship between worlds: including debt, freedom, race, rights, the human, and value.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Ethnographic Research Methods: Ethics and Engagement
courses.description: Interrogation of ethnographic research, its development and its ethical implications. Weighing approaches such as participatory action research, engaged and collaborative research, and decolonized methodologies. Students will develop projects based on a critical reading of these models.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Behavioral Ecology of Hunter Gatherers
courses.description: A thorough introduction using a behavioral ecology approach to the diversity of behaviors found among foragers in Africa, South America, Southeast Asia, and Australia. Topics include: diet and subsistence, mating, demography, social behavior, mobility and settlement patterns, gender, indigenous rights, and conservation.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: International Development and Population Health
courses.description: Considers the distribution and determinants of well being in human populations, with an emphasis on low-income nations and the actions of the international development sector. Focus is placed on cultural/social determinants of health, including issues of gender equality. Takes a critical perspective on the tools used to measure population health and the design and evaluation of development policy and interventions.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Anthropology of Law
courses.description: Examines the way the law and legal apparatuses binds subjects (human and otherwise) to the material world. It does so by conceptually analyzing what the law is and the experiences it creates as they are depicted in legal discourse, the historical archive, and ethnography. Topics include rights, freedoms, and entitlements; crime and punishment; slavery and servitude; the formation of constitutional power; status laws and the logic of race that undergirds them; and the subterranean political, social, and economic desires that the law seeks to exploit and animate within “the people.”

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Cultural Development in Mesoamerica
courses.comments: Offered periodically.
courses.description: The rise and fall of various ancient civilizations such as those of the Maya, Aztecs, Toltecs, Teotihuacanos, and Olmec as well as their cultural antecedents. This course uses self-paced audiovisual modules as well as traditional lecture format.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Cultural Anthropology of Latin America
courses.description: Contemporary issues of rural and urban societies in the Caribbean, and Central and South America. Examination of continuities and changes in cultural institutions and values; inequality, colonialism, settler colonialism, state formation, indigenous social movements, race, gender, class and ethnicity, urbanization, extractivism.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Interdisciplinary Approaches to the History and Societies of Latin America and Iberia
courses.comments: ANTH 134A, LAIS 101, and SPAN 107 are the same course. LAIS 101S is a legal repeat of ANTH 134A, LAIS 101, and SPAN 107.
courses.description: Issues central to the study of Latin America and Iberia across the social sciences and history. Topics include nationalism, revolution, politics and the state, economic development and international relations, labor, popular culture, race, gender, religion, migration, environment, imperialism, and colonialism.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Cultural Anthropology of Mexico
courses.description: An examination of contemporary issues in Mexico through an anthropological lens. Topics may include race, class, gender, and sexuality, nation-state formation, settler colonialism, decolonization, social movements, and political economy.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Language and Social Signs
courses.description: Explores a tradition of anthropological inquiry that builds an account of language as a system of socially intelligible signs. Often referred to as semiotics, this class examines how signs and language become the conduits for thinking about and understanding our relationship with the world, our shared social and political ecologies, and how our interpretation of such signs is expressive of larger structures that lie inside of us. Topics and concepts for exploration include the relationship between language, signs, and symbols; structuralism and poststructuralism; performativity and performance; practice and action; ontology and metaphysics; discourse and discursive agency; and speech and communicative rationality.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: The Ancient Maya
courses.description: The splendiferous Maya civilization as it waxed and waned during ancient times.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Anthropology of Environmental Health
courses.prereq_text: ANTH 2 or equivalent introduction to sociocultural anthropology
courses.description: A sociocultural medical anthropological approach to explore how environmental hazards, many of them human-influenced, shape health and illness around the world. Topics include environmental risk and perception, industrial toxics, disasters, environmental justice, and chronic disease.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Land of the Pharaohs: An Archaeology of Ancient Egypt
courses.description: Selected topics on the archaeology of ancient Egypt, placing the monuments of this great civilization in the context of its rise and development. Emphasis on ancient Egyptian material culture as a source for understanding Egyptian political, social, and economic dynamics.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Landback, Reparations, and Solidarity Economies
courses.description: An introduction to two related topics that have become increasingly central in the US and beyond in recent years: rising demands for, and concrete steps toward, the return of lands to present day descendants of Native and Indigenous peoples who previously occupied these lands [colloquially known as "land back"]; and the payment of reparations [either monetary or in kind] to descendants of enslaved peoples, as partial compensation for the trauma, social suffering and economic loss of enslavement. We critically examine the arguments put forth to justify both flows of thought and action; we study actual cases where these actions have been taken; and we ask what can be learned.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Ethics in Archaeology
courses.description: An analysis of ethics in contemporary archaeology. Topics include reburial and repatriation, interpretation of the archaeological record in the context of historically oppressed groups, ethnic minorities, and non-western societies. The course also includes the ethics of collecting and managing cultural property.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Anthropological Demography and Life History
courses.prereq_text: Anthropology 5 or 7 or upper-division standing; or Environmental Studies 2 or 3.
courses.description: Introduces students to anthropologic applications of demography and life history theory. Focuses on ecological approaches to population dynamics, birth and death processes, and policy implications in light of population "problems" among traditional and modern societies.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Water and Society
courses.comments: Anthropology 147 and Environmental Studies 138 are the same course.
courses.description: Covers the longstanding debate over the relation between irrigation and state formation, as well as current developments in the study of water and society. Emphasis is placed on people living in arid and semi-arid environments.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Human Genetics
courses.prereq_text: ANTH 5 or ANTH 7, ANTH 9 or equivalent.
courses.description: Introduction to basic principles of genetics and genomics in human evolution. Topics covered include molecular evolution, population genetics, comparative genomics, epigenetics, gene-culture interactions and relevant social and ethical issues.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Evolutionary Psychology
courses.description: Surveys evolutionary psychology, examining traditional psychological topics through Darwinian lenses. Traditional psychology answers mechanistic questions about how perception, emotion, cognition, development and social interactions work. Evolutionary psychology addresses the complementary functional question of why they work the way they do.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Environmental Anthropology
courses.comments: Same Course as ENV S 151
courses.description: Examines the ways that humans interact with, use, and perceive the environment and nature, with a focus on the cultural, political, and economic features of human environment relationships across time and in different parts of the world. Through readings, in-class activities and discussions, field trips, and research projects, students will gain a better understanding of how anthropological theory, research, and applications can be used to address contemporary environment topics and problems.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Primate Behavior
courses.prereq_text: Anthropology 5 or 7; not open to freshmen.
courses.description: An introduction to primatology and the principles of behavioral ecology using langur, vervet, macaque, baboon, gorilla, and chimpanzee field studies to illustrate theories of foraging, parenting, kinship, sexual selection, incest avoidance, aggression, and dominance. Concludes with applications to human evolution.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: The Anthropology of Africa
courses.description: This course offers an overview of the anthropological studies of people on the African continent. Drawing from case studies in archaeology, historical linguistics, ethnography, biological anthropology and medical anthropology, this course documents a sea change from Africa under the gaze of the West, to Africa as examined and defined by African peoples from their own diverse and varied perspectives.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Ethnographic Field Methods
courses.comments: Misc: May be repeated two times provided content is different.
courses.description: Introduction to skills and tools of data collection through fieldwork in cultural anthropology. Emphasis on techniques, methods, and concepts of ethnographic research and how basic observational information is systematized for presentation, analysis, and cross-cultural comparison.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Anthropology of War
courses.description: Examines the concepts and experiences that cohere around warfare and weaponized conflict. Investigates the modern shape of war, its technologies, its strategies and how it’s infused within broader political and social life. Topics and concepts include military, civil, political, and social violence; insurgency and counterinsurgency; revolution and counterrevolution; enmity and the logics of race; power and force; sovereignty and territorial space; security and protection; and communicative reason and the lack thereof.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Prehistoric Food Production
courses.description: A history of the process of plant and animal domestication in the Americas, the Near East, Asia, and Africa. Course focuses on the specific biological changes in the major domesticates as well as associated social changes in human life.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: The Origins of Complex Societies
courses.description: Why and how complex societies developed from simple, egalitarian societies in some areas of the world. Course surveys major theories and evidence surrounding the origins of states and urban societies in New and Old World.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: People of the Ice Age
courses.description: Human adaptations and population dispersals during the Ice Age (Pleistocene epoch). Course focuses on Stone Age cultures and the evidence for early human occupation of the Americas and the Old World between three million and 10,000 years ago.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Evolution of Cooperation
courses.description: Interdisciplinary focus on the emergence and maintenance of cooperation in human populations. Are we unique in our abilities to reap gains from cooperative endeavors? Why are some people generous, others stingy? How do propensities, personalities, ecology, and cultural institutions affect success in cooperation?

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: The Evolutionary Anthropology of Family Life
courses.description: Explores how evolutionary anthropologists study cultural diversity in human family life. Together we examine global variation in marriage systems, kinship and inheritance rules, parental investment, norms of sex and reproduction, and the role of extended kin. Each week pairs human examples with insights from non-human animals to ask what evolutionary theory reveals about the determinants of family structure, adaptation to local environments, and patterns of conflict and cooperation among family members.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Evolutionary Medicine
courses.prereq_text: Anth 5 with a minimum grade of C; or, EEMB 2 and EEMB 3; or, MCDB 1 and MCDB 2.
courses.description: Applies evolutionary principles to understanding human health and disease past and present. Topics include host/parasite co-evolution, aging and senescence, influence of human migration and culture on disease patterns, and evolutionary origins of diseases of civilization."

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Amazonia
courses.description: Focuses on the people, environment, and history of Amazon basin. Topics of study include human-environment interactions across time; social and cultural groups; representations in film, media, and literature; and contemporary social, political, and environmental issues facing the region.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Medical Anthropology
courses.description: This sociocultural anthropology course is focused on the social construction of health, risk, illness, and disease in the US and around the globe and research methods used to study them. Topics include health inequality and its social production, critical analysis of biomedicine and power, technologies of diagnosis and treatment, stigma and disability, gender, bodies and health, mental health and illness, medicalization and pharmaceuticalization, and global health and humanitarian care.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Temples, Tombs and Hieroglyphs: Ancient Egyptian Religion
courses.description: Examination of Ancient Egyptian religion from massive temples and pyramids to modest offerings and simple burials. The interaction of sacred and secular is considered through examination of the individual, society, and the state in shaping religious beliefs.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Human Reproduction Ecology and Endocrinology
courses.description: Regulation of reproductive function by diet, energy balance, lactation, and social context. The role of hormones in the regulation of human reproduction, behavior, and physiology. Hormonal changes with parenting and pregnancy in men and women.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Internship in Archaeological Record-Keeping and Collections
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 4 units.
courses.description: Interns serve as assistants in the department's Central Coast Information Center or Repository for Archaeological Collections or both.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Archaeology of Ethnicity & Race
courses.description: Concepts of ethnicity and race are catalyzing forces today. Exploring the changing definitions and resonances of these categories in an archaeological context, we examine how these concepts shifted in antiquity and modern scholarship, with particular reference to Egypt, Nubia, and the Mediterranean.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Introduction to Lithic Analysis
courses.description: This course gives students an introduction to the anthropology and archaeology of making and using stone tools. Practical experience in making tools and using them experimentally is emphasized.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Internship in Archaeological Resource Management
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 4 units.
courses.description: Interns serve as assistants or trainees in the archaeological programs of a governmental agency, a museum, or a private firm in the local area. In collaboration with the instructor and an extramural archaeologist, the student conceives a set of activities for the internship.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Lab Course in Paleoethnobotany
courses.description: Study of archaeological plant remains, including field/lab methodology, the reconstruction of ancient environment and the subsistence, spatial and temporal analysis, quantitative methods, and taxonomy. Divided between lecture, discussion, and labwork, involving microscopic identification of paleoethnobotanical remains.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Lab Course in Zooarchaeology
courses.description: Study of archaeological faunal remains, including field/lab methodology, the reconstruction of ancient environment and the subsistence, spatial and temporal analysis, quantitative methods, and taxonomy. Divided between lecture, discussion, and labwork, involving identification of zooarchaeological remains.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Problems in European Prehistory
courses.description: Seminar in selected problems in the archaeology of Europe.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Cultural Anthropology Internship
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 8 units but only 4 units may be applied to major.
courses.description: Students serve as interns in various settings such as museums, governmental agencies, and health organizations to gain exposure to different cultures. In collaboration with the instructor and an extramural anthropologist, the student conceives a set of activities for the internship.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: After graduation: Preparing for Graduate School and the Job Market
courses.prereq_text: Juniors and Seniors only; limited to Anthropology Majors/Minors
courses.comments: Juniors and Seniors only; limited to Anthropology Majors/Minors
courses.description: This course is designed to guide students: (1) through the graduate school application process, and (2) in how to prepare for the job market. We will consider all steps and components of applying to graduate school. The second half of class will focus on best practices for finding jobs after graduation.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Field Training Archaeology
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units, but only 8 units may be applied toward the major
courses.description: Introduction to design of research projects and techniques of data collection in archaeology. The number of units taken in one course will depend on the amount of training and experience received.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Practicum in Field and Laboratory Analysis
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit; however, only 6 units may be applied to Anthropology major requirements.
courses.description: An applied course emphasizing acquisition of practical skills in archaeological field work and laboratory analysis. Projects will vary depending on the type of archaeological research in progress and may include artifact processing, cataloguing, field excavation and preparation of research results.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Anthropology Honors Program: Research Design
courses.prereq_text: Admission to Anthropology honors program; consent of instructor.
courses.description: Formal classroom seminar to prepare students for the ANTH 195B and 195C Anthropology honors thesis sequence. This course guides students in formulating a research problem that they will pursue in ANTH 195B and 195C, including planning a research agenda and conducting background research that will frame their honors thesis project. Project completion will be carried out individually during ANTH 195B and 195C.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Anthropology Honors Program: INDIVIDUAL STUDY PART I
courses.prereq_text: Admission to Anthropology Honors Program; consent of instructor; ANTH 195A
courses.description: Individual research under the supervision of an Anthropology faculty member which will result in an honorsthesis. This course concentrates on reading and gathering of materials for thesis.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Anthropology Honors Program: INDIVIDUAL STUDY PART II
courses.description: Individual research under the supervision of an Anthropology faculty member which results in an honors thesis. Writing the thesis will be completed in this course. Final course in progress series.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Special Courses
courses.comments: May be repeated two times provided content is different.
courses.description: Intensive studies or projects focused on special problems related to Anthropology which are not covered by other courses.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Special Courses
courses.comments: May be repeated two times provided content is different.
courses.description: Intensive studies or projects focused on special problems related to Anthropology which are not covered by other courses.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Biology of Women
courses.comments: May be repeated two times provided content is different.
courses.description: An exploration of female and womxn’s reproductive lives from an evolutionary and biocultural perspective. We will focus on physiological, ecological, and social aspects of womxn’s development across cultures from before birth, through reproductive processes like pregnancy, birth, lactation, menopause, and aging. Examples will be drawn from contemporary human societies, including many small-scale societies, although non-human primates will also be considered occasionally. This class will include lectures, discussion in multiple formats, and other modes of learning. Recommended Prep: ANTH 5 or Equivalent ANTH Majors: Take for Letter Grade to apply for Major Requirements

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Caring for Transformation: The Affect of Social Justice
courses.comments: May be repeated two times provided content is different.
courses.description: This course recognizes the emotional effects of oppression. Recently, more attention shows how systemic mistreatment of people affects the social and economic wellbeing of communities (both systematically targeted by racism and colonization and those enforcing these systems). We will practice, reflect, discuss, and explore what healing from oppression looks like. We explore the emotional dimensions of oppression and justice while being aware that the history of injustice is full of intense emotions. How do we connect the personal, academic, and political experience of living and researching through these experiences? How do we analyze and heal the effects of injustice and mistreatment and support our academic practice and activist work?

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Sensory Ecologies
courses.comments: May be repeated two times provided content is different.
courses.description: This seminar critically examines how sensory experiences mediate various kinds of relationships, including between humans, nonhumans, and environments. Drawing from anthropology, science and technology studies (STS), environmental humanities, art theory and practice, and sensory ethnography, the course explores how ecologies are lived, perceived, created, and contested through embodied practice. We will analyze how sensory regimes are shaped by power hierarchies, labor, infrastructures, and histories, and how they inform knowledge production, governance, resistance, refusal, and creative endeavors. Students will engage multimodal methods to investigate how ecological relations, broadly conceived, are felt, negotiated, and made meaningful.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Special Courses
courses.comments: May be repeated two times provided content is different.
courses.description: Intensive studies or projects focused on special problems related to Anthropology which are not covered by other courses.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Field Methods in Biocultural Anthropology
courses.comments: May be repeated two times provided content is different.
courses.description: Research design and data collection are skills that are necessary for all researchers to propose and conduct successful research projects. The primary aims of this course are (1) to familiarize students with the process of designing a research project, (2) to introduce students to a variety of data collection methods typically used by cultural and biological anthropologists, as well as other social scientists, and (3) to provide students with hands-on experience and thorough feedback on designing and conducting their own projects.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Pathways of Indigenous Laws in Mexico
courses.comments: May be repeated two times provided content is different.
courses.description: In this seminar, students take part in the research design of a survey research project in collaboration with an Organization of Indigenous Lawyers in Oaxaca. We analyze the interviews and fieldnotes of research conducted during June 2025 in Oaxaca, with indigenous authorities and other state authorities. In the class, students learn about the legal system in Mexico, Indigenous Customary Law, the discrimination faced by indigenous people in the legal system, and conflict resolution. Along with text analysis, coding and survey design.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: The Science of Friendship
courses.comments: May be repeated two times provided content is different.
courses.description: Why are friendships so central to our daily lives? This class explores the causes and consequences of this fundamental human bond, traversing its roots in animal behavior, its underlying biology and psychology, its relationship with health, and both its diversity and universal features across human cultures.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Independent Readings in Anthropology
courses.prereq_text: Upper-division standing; completion of 2 upper-division courses in Anthropology.
courses.comments: Students must have a minimum 3.0 GPA for the preceding 3 quarters and are limited to 5 units per quarter and 30 units total in all 98/99/198/199/199AA-ZZ courses combined. May be repeated to a maximum of 12 units in Anthropology.
courses.description: Intended for students who know their own reading needs. Normally requires regular meeting with the instructor.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Independent Studies in Anthropology
courses.prereq_text: Upper-division standing; completion of 2 upper-division courses in Anthropology.
courses.comments: Students must have a minimum 3.0 GPA for the preceding 3 quarters and are limited to 5 units per quarter and 30 units total in all 98/99/198/199/199AA-ZZ courses combined. May be repeated to a maximum of 12 units in Anthropology.
courses.description: Students must execute a limited research project on their own initiative.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Undergraduate Research Assistance Training in Anthropology
courses.prereq_text: Upper-division standing; completion of 2 upper-division courses in Anthropology.
courses.comments: Students must have a minimum 3.0 GPA for the preceding 3 quarters and are limited to 5 units per quarter and 30 units total in all 98/99/198/199/199AA-ZZ courses combined. May be repeated to maximum of 12 units.
courses.description: Student gains research experience through assisting faculty member in research project.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Classical Archaeological Theory
courses.comments: Not open for credit to students who have completed Anthropology 201.
courses.description: A survey and critique of archaeological theory from the nineteenth century through the 1970's, with emphasis on shifting paradigms and the implications for research.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Contemporary Archaeology Theory
courses.comments: Not open for credit to students who have completed Anthropology 201.
courses.description: A survey and critique or archaeological theory from the 1980's to the present, emphasizing the diversity of new approaches and their implications for research.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Race, Racism, and Anti-racism in Anthropology
courses.description: A critical review of Anthropology's engagements with race, racism, and anti-racism, past and present.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Ethics and the Profession of Anthropology
courses.description: A critical review of political and legal issues involved in the practice of anthropology, past and present.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Current Problems in Archaeology
courses.comments: Course may be repeated for credit.
courses.description: Critical examination of a selected aspect of contemporary archaeological research and theory. Topics will vary from year to year.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Current Problems in Archaeology
courses.comments: Course may be repeated for credit.
courses.description: Critical examination of a selected aspect of contemporary archaeological research and theory. Topics will vary from year to year.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Current Problems in Archaeology
courses.comments: Course may be repeated for credit.
courses.description: Critical examination of a selected aspect of contemporary archaeological research and theory. Topics will vary from year to year.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Anthropological Political Economy
courses.description: A Marxist perspective on topics such as: state formation, infrastructure, accumulation, neoliberalism, culture and class, land and labor, structure and process.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Applying Evolutionary Anthropology
courses.description: Exploratory discussion of the potential of evolutionary anthropology to critique and inform the actions of the international development sector.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: The Origins and Intensification of Agriculture
courses.description: Focuses on the origins and intensification of agriculture, by examining the shifts from foraging to farming to intensive food production. We consider issues of risk and uncertainty, timing relative to political complexity, population increase/nucleation, warfare, among other issues.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Ethnicity and Race in the Americas
courses.description: Identifies different racial projects, of how "ethnicity" and "race" are understood in specific contexts. Special attention is put on the ideas of mestizaje, indigenismo and development, and the role that played in the racial projects of Latin America.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Liberalism and War
courses.description: The course begins from the assumption that liberalism is a paradigmatic condition that defines the boundaries between life and death through its inextricable relationship to war. The course proceeds to explore this condition structurally, focusing on the economic, legal, political, and social forms generated from liberalism’s war power. This includes forms expressed in the flows of capital, the legal binds of secularism, securitization and counterinsurgency, the formation of the police power, and the management of the impending ecological catastrophe. Course topics examine foundational concepts that collocate war and liberalism: including sovereignty, value, freedom, human life, rights, secularization, force, and the state form.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Advanced Theory and Method in Evolutionary Psychology
courses.description: Interdepartmental research practicum in evolutionary psychology, biology, and anthropology for students and faculty planning or working on evolutionary research projects. Focus on experimental design, cross-cultural methods, organism design theory, new adaptationist hypotheses, and the criteria for testing them.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Foundations of Modern Social Theory
courses.description: Seminar introduces major post-enlightenment debates on social life and modernity. Selections from Marx, Durkheim, Weber, Freud as well as major responses, revisions and critiques in critical and subaltern theory, cultural studies, structuralism and poststructuralism. Close readings of primary texts emphasized.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Issues in Contemporary Anthropology
courses.description: Survey of major theoretical trends since the 1960's. Topics include: political economy and Marxism; evolution, history, and anthropology; symbolic anthropology; development studies; gender studies; colonialism and nationalism; structuralism/post-structuralism; modernity and post-modernity; ecological anthropology. Topics may vary with each professor.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Research Design and Writing in Archaeology
courses.description: How to design a fieldwork project and write a dissertation research proposal; the search for funding agencies; how to deal with funding institutions, professional organizations, publishers and employers; issues of a career in anthropology.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Research Methods in Cultural Anthropology
courses.description: Designed to give students a solid grounding in basic research methods in cultural anthropology. Focus on the role of fieldwork, preparation for field research (ethics, health, and gender), systematic data collection, qualitative data base management and analysis.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Research Design and Writing in Sociocultural Anthropology
courses.description: How to design a fieldwork project and write a dissertation research proposal; the search for funding agencies; how to deal with funding institutions, professional organizations, publishers and employers; issues of a career in anthropology.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Contemporary Topics in Biological Anthropology
courses.prereq_text: Graduate standing in Anthropology or a related field.
courses.description: Read and discuss professional literature in biological anthropology and related fields: evolutionary and life history theory, human biology, paleoanthropology, biomedical science and primatology. Course keeps students abreast of key developments in the field.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Current Findings in Biological Anthropology
courses.description: Open to graduate students in biological anthropology and allied fields, this course reviews research findings in human evolutionary studies.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Current Methods in Biological Anthropology
courses.description: Open to graduate students in biological anthropology and allied fields, this course reviews research methods in human evolutionary studies.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Pedagogical Methods and Strategies in Biological Anthropology
courses.description: Primarily for graduate students in other subfields of anthropology, to help them master effective methods for teaching biological anthropology at the undergraduate level.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Anthropological Demography and Life History
courses.description: Core concepts of demography are covered, including theory and methods related to fertility, mortality and population dynamics. Themes include aging, maternal and child health, demographic and epidemiological transitions. Lecture with class discussions.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Quantitative Data Analysis Archaeology
courses.description: This course is and introduction to the practical analysis of commonly-encountered archaeological data using simple quantitative and statistical procedures, such as exploratory data analysis, sampling, regression, and spatial analysis. The course is taught in a computer-assisted (multimedia) format.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Evolutionary Anthropology Lab
courses.description: Weekly discussion of IAS faculty and graduate student work in progress

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Method and Theory in Anthropology
courses.description: A discussion of general problems in anthropology. Consult with department office for faculty designation.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Method and Theory in Anthropology
courses.description: A discussion of general problems in anthropology. Consult with department office for faculty designation.

courses.description: A discussion of general problems in anthropology. Consult with department office for faculty designation.

courses.title: Method and Theory in Anthropology
courses.description: A discussion of general problems in anthropology. Consult with department office for faculty designation.

courses.title: Method and Theory in Anthropology
courses.description: A discussion of general problems in anthropology. Consult with department office for faculty designation.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Political Ecology
courses.description: Study of human - environment interactions with attention to power, agency, and multi-scalar connections.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Surveillance
courses.description: Looks at surveillance in anthropology and related social studies/humanistic disciplines. Engages work on observing, the power dynamics of watching and being watched, and technologies of surveying and surveillance—from colonial ethnography to contemporary regimes of data collection. Readings examine state surveillance, policing, bureaucracy, and digital platforms, alongside less formal practices of monitoring embedded in care, labor regimes, humanitarianism, and everyday life. Emphasizing ethnographic approaches, the course attends to how surveillance is lived, felt, and unevenly distributed. Also explores refusal, protest, opacity, and counter-surveillance as political and ethical responses.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Theories of Mestizaje: Critical Perspectives from the Americas
courses.description: Mestizaje has been one of the longest racial projects in the American continent, both as a de facto phenomena and as an ideology. This course critically engages with contemporary debates. Explores Mestizaje as resistance, as well as domination.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Culture Contact and Interaction
courses.description: Examination of culture's role in human history, with an emphasis on how the combination of archaeological, historical, ethnohistorical and ethnographic data can yield insights into the dynamics of interactions between different groups at various times and places.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: M.A. Paper Preparation
courses.description: Required research and writing seminar during which second-year graduate students write individual M.A. papers.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Teaching Assistant Practicum
courses.comments: Appointment as teaching assistant in anthropology. No unit credit allowed toward degree.
courses.description: The course, designed to meet the needs of the graduate student who serves as a teaching assistant, includes analyses of texts and materials, discussion of teaching techniques, conducting discussion sections, formulation of topics and questions for papers and examinations, and grading papers and examinations under the supervision of the instructor assigned to the course.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Field Research Training
courses.comments: (Possibly) offered concurrently with Anthropology 194.
courses.description: Introduction to the planning and implementation of full-scale research projects. The opportunity will be given to formulate and carry out designs and to direct crews in data collection.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Directed Reading and Research
courses.comments: No more than half the graduate units necessary for the Master's degree may be taken in 596.
courses.description: Individual tutorial.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Individual Study for Master's Comprehensive Examinations
courses.comments: No unit credit allowed toward degree.
courses.description: Individual tutorial.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Master's Thesis and Pre-Candidacy Preparation
courses.comments: No credit allowed toward degree.
courses.description: Individual tutorial for graduate students writing the research paper and/or dissertation proposal for advancement to candidacy.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Dissertation Research and Preparation
courses.comments: No unit credit allowed toward degree.
courses.description: Individual tutorial.

courses.subject: ANTH W
courses.title: World Archaeology
courses.description: An introduction to archaeology and the history of humankind from the earliest times through the advent of literate civilization and cities, also processes of cultural change and the importance of archaeology to people and societies today. Partly self-paced learning.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Visual Literacy
courses.description: An introductory survey of visual culture, encompassing art and film theory and practice, digital technologies, television, advertising and print media, with a special focus on current interdisciplinary methodologies.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Introduction to Contemporary Art
courses.description: Symposium format course presents contemporary artists' creative projects in relation to recent developments in art and cross-disciplinary practices. Lectures by UCSB's Art Department faculty and also distinguished guests invited to expand on art, theory and cultural production.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: The Intersections of Art and Life
courses.comments: Course materials fee charged
courses.description: Explores art in relation to time-based activity and integration with everyday life. Conceptual introduction to authorship, authenticity, and narrative through exercises and examples of performance, video, film, book, arts, sound, digital media, and interactive/chance derived work.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Introduction to Contemporary Practice I: Image Studies
courses.comments: Course materials fee charged
courses.description: The study of visual perception and image-making across visual art disciplines, both material and digital. Studio assignments are combined with related critical theory, historical practice, current strategies, and new evolutions.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Introduction to Contemporary Practice II: Spatial Studies
courses.comments: Course materials fee charged
courses.description: The study of spatial art in many forms, including material, interactive and dynamic digital. Studio assignments are combined with related critical theory, historical practice, current strategies and new evolutions.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Introduction to Contemporary Practice III: Art, Science and Technologies
courses.comments: Course materials fee charged
courses.description: The study of foundations of digital and technological arts in all forms, including history, theory and practice of optical, kinetic, interactive, interdisciplinary and systems-oriented art. Lectures and assignments introduce concepts, methods, movements and practitioners that have shaped the fields.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Introduction to Painting
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 8 units, but only 4 units can be applied to the major. Course materials fee charged.
courses.description: Traditional and contemporary painting assignments designed to provide a strong foundation in fundamental 2D image making. Media include acrylic and oil painting methods.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Beginning Spatial Practices
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 8 units but only 4 units can be applied to the major. Course materials fee charged.
courses.description: Introduction to the challenges, strategies, and techniques of 3D artmaking within the expanding fields of traditional and contemporary sculpture.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Lower-Division Print
courses.comments: Open to non-majors. May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 8 units but only 4 units can be applied to the major. Letter grade required for majors. Course materials fee charged.
courses.description: Introduction to making prints. Emphasis on technical fundamentals and conceptual aspects of graphic arts. "Print" incorporates hand produced mechanically or photographically reproduced, and electronically replicated media.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Lower-Division Drawing
courses.comments: Letter grade required for majors. May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 8 units but only 4 units can be applied to the major. Open to non-majors. Course materials fee charged.
courses.description: Introduction to two-dimensional representation with various drawing media, including structural and symbolic implications of the human form. Emphasis on organization of vision and thought.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Lower-Division Photography
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 8 units, but only 4 units can be applied to the major.
courses.description: Introduction to photography-based image-making that may include still photography, new approaches to documentary, online projects, explorations in visual narrative, mixed media, social and public practices. Instruction in digital imagine and printing.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Introduction to Computer Programming in the Arts
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 8 units, but only 4 units may be applied to the major.
courses.description: Using a project-based approach, the basic components of web development and computer programming are explored in different markup and programming languages such as HTML/CSS, JavaScript, and Processing. The class is intended to create a general understanding of computer programming, its use and cultural implications, as well as provide a foundation for utilizing programming in a wide range of projects, from traditional to new media.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Introduction to Digital Video
courses.description: Introduction to digital video production including camera work, editing, sound, and distribution platforms. Conceptual and technical concerns relevant to video in the evolving theater of contemporary art and culture.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Intermediate Contemporary Painting Issues
courses.prereq_text: Art 10; Art 1A or 7B or Upper Division standing or Instructor Approval
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units with instructor approval. Letter grade required for majors. Course materials fee charged.
courses.description: Various projects designed to assist the understanding and development of contemporary painting practices. Supplemented with slide lectures and class critique. Additional self-directed projects, sketch books, experimentation, and independent research are encouraged.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Advanced Contemporary Painting Issues
courses.prereq_text: Art 10,100; 1A or 7B or Upper Division standing or Instructor Approval
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units. Course materials fee charged.
courses.description: Special critique-based class addressing current issues in contemporary painting. 'Painting' will be used in broadest sense including traditional methods, and digital painting (digitally manipulated images as source), installation and inter-media practices utilizing paint as dominant medium.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Digital Media Tool Box: Concepts and Skills
courses.prereq_text: Art 22, 7D; 1A or Upper Division or Instructor Approval
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units.
courses.description: A project based course with an emphasis on technical skills within the digital media arts context. Topics may include telecommunications, wireless, database aesthetics, networks, interactivity, digital 3D, virtual reality, immersive environments, algorithmic aesthetics, visualization, media theory and others. Topic to be determined by instructor.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Digital Project: Mobile Media
courses.prereq_text: Art 22, 7D; 1A or Upper Division or Instructor Approval
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units.
courses.description: In this class we will make mobile app art projects for smartphones and tablets using HTML/CSS, JavaScript and Perl. Through the conceptualization and creation of these projects, we investigate social and locative media, ubiquity, the possibilities and limits of apps as art and the cultural implications of the increased uses of mobile apps. Students will also learn basic programming skills that can be applied towards learning and using other computer languages for a wide range of purposes.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Intermediate Spatial Practices
courses.prereq_text: Art 12; 1A or 7C or Upper Division or Instructor Approval
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units with instructor approval. Letter-grade required for majors. Course materials fee charged.
courses.description: Designed to develop student knowledge and proficiency of material and method, cultivating both manual and conceptual skill-levels in three-dimensional practices. Course focus varies by quarter, but includes a variety of approaches to material practices and engages students in the role of spatial awareness and production within contemporary art.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Intermediate Spatial Practices - Public Practice
courses.prereq_text: Art 12; 1A or 7C or Upper Division or Instructor Approval
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units with instructor approval. Letter-grade required for majors.
courses.description: Developing your own voice in sculpture and installation while considering your audience is central to this course. Each student is encouraged to work with existing skills and build new ones in exploratory, materially fascinating works. At least one of your works will be situated in the public realm. We examine recent public art practices, cultivating manual, conceptual and collaborative skills in both the studio and public realm.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Intermediate Spatial Practices
courses.prereq_text: Art 12; 1A or 7C or Upper Division or Instructor Approval
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units with instructor approval. Letter-grade required for majors. Course materials fee charged.
courses.description: Designed to develop student knowledge and proficiency of material and method, cultivating both manual and conceptual skill-levels in three-dimensional practices. Course focus varies by quarter, but includes a variety of approaches to material practices and engages students in the role of spatial awareness and production within contemporary art.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Intermediate Spatial Practices: Physical & Virtual
courses.prereq_text: Art 12; 1A or 7C or Upper Division or Instructor Approval
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units with instructor approval. Letter-grade required for majors.
courses.description: This project-based experimental studio explores foundational concepts of 3D form through ceramics, 3D printing, and 3D scanning. Students move fluidly between hand-building clay and digital fabrication processes, collaborating with computers, machines, and physical toolsets to translate ideas into objects while examining relationships between bodies, materials, and hybrid analog–digital workflows. Emphasizing ceramics as a site of dialogue between primitive and emerging technologies, the course encourages students to develop personal and political approaches to form beyond traditional 3D modeling.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Advanced Spatial Practices
courses.prereq_text: Art 12; 1A or 7C or Upper Division or Instructor Approval
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units. Letter grade required for majors. Course materials fee charged.
courses.description: Advanced study and investigation of new forms and spatial practices. Individual and group projects may encompass formal and collaborative research as well as multi-disciplinary production that engages new and exploratory practices, such as interactive and performative media, public art, social design at the intersection of architecture, urbanism and contemporary art. Course content detailed in syllabus each quarter.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Introduction to 2D/3D Visualizations in Architecture
courses.prereq_text: Upper-division standing; open to majors only.
courses.comments: Same course as Art History 136W.
courses.description: Develops skills in reading, interpreting, and visualizing 3D objects and spaces by offering exercises in sketching, perspective, orthographic projections, isometric drawings, and manual rendering practices. Relevant for those interested in history of architecture, sculpture, and such spatial practices as installations and public art.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Intermediate Print
courses.prereq_text: Art 14, 18; 1A or 7B or Upper Division or Instructor Approval
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units. Course materials fee charged.
courses.description: Continued refinement of skills in service of ink and digital print production. Emphasis on intermedia aspects of image and text and the sequential use of pictorial information. Areas of specific focus to include electronic multiples, relief printing, and artists' books.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Public Practice Arts: Digital Intermedia
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units.
courses.description: The use of digital and print-based media to create site-responsive public projects including unsanctioned, permission based, and speculative works. The investigation of the evolving nature and use of public space and its interrelations of individual, social, architectural/built, and infrastructure conditions. Projects are executed both on and off campus.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Artists' Books
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units.
courses.description: An investigation of the book as an art form. Based on conventional media, artists' books encompass a variety of methods, techniques, and ideas. Assigned and self-directed projects using traditional and innovative practices, combining reading with pictorial and tactile experience.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Experimental Video & Animation
courses.description: The development of independent, innovative projects that utilize digital video and/or post-production and hybrid means to create video-works for screens and surfaces, including projection, installation, distributed platforms. Projects may employ a variety of strategies and methodologies in concept, production, and presentation. Broad exposure to contemporary and pioneering video/film, with an emphasis on experimentation in substance and form.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Intermediate Drawing
courses.prereq_text: Art 18; 1A or 7B or Upper Division or Instructor Approval
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units with instructor approval. Course materials fee charged.
courses.description: Continuing investigation into the challenges of two-dimensional representation. Course focus to depend on instructor, but may include structural and symbolic implications of the human form, historical and contemporary strategies of visual analysis, and exploration into experimental media.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Advanced Drawing
courses.prereq_text: Art 18, 117; 1A or Upper Division or Instructor Approval
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units. Letter grade required for majors. Course materials fee charged.
courses.description: Special studies in drawing utilizing particular faculty interests and/or special departmental facilities. Designed for majors.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Intermediate Photography
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units with instructor approval. Letter grade required for majors. Course materials fee charged.
courses.description: Continued refinement of traditional photographic technique, and development of photography as an artmaking tool. Course to range by instructor, but may include photo narrative, journalism, fashion, artists' books, desktop publishing, web design, time-based work, and intermedia collaborations.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Intermediate Photography
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units with instructor approval. Letter grade required for majors.
courses.description: Students will conceptualize, research, and propose narrative photography projects that focus on telling a visual story. Development and production of projects will include investigation of methods in which photography can describe: time, causality, dramatic composition, spatiality, fictional and non-fictional story telling, etc.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Intermediate Photography - Photographing People
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units with instructor approval. Letter grade required for majors.
courses.description: Photographing People is a course for people who want to photograph people and communities. Through creative practice, methods, and critical approaches students tell profound visual stories in the visual genre of their personal artistic pursuit. Course work culminates in a photographic project.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Advanced Topics in Digital Media
courses.prereq_text: Art 22, 7D; 1A or Upper Division or Instructor Approval
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units.
courses.description: An advanced project based course in digital media arts. Students are expected to have relevant conceptual, aesthetic, and technological grounding in digital media. Topic to be determined by instructor.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Advanced Topics in Digital Media
courses.prereq_text: Art 22, 7D; 1A or Upper Division or Instructor Approval
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units.
courses.description: An advanced project based course in digital media arts. Students are expected to have relevant conceptual, aesthetic, and technological grounding in digital media. Topic to be determined by instructor.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Advanced Digital Projects: Physical Computing
courses.prereq_text: Art 22, 7D; 1A or Upper Division or Instructor Approval
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units.
courses.description: Explores experimental approaches to designing, prototyping, and building human-centered interactive systems through the lens of weaving as both structure and computation. Tracing the history of computing from its origins in loom technologies and textile production to contemporary electronic and smart textiles, students investigate how woven systems inform wearable technology, kinetic objects, circuit design, and the integration of electronics with software using conductive thread, yarn, and soft circuitry. Drawing from fiber arts, performance, architecture, sustainability, and speculative design, the course positions weaving as a foundational model for understanding and reimagining embodied human interaction with technology.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Art Since 1950
courses.description: Developments in American and European art since 1950 with an emphasis on the most recent decades. Focus ranges from the post-war impact of the New York School, Pop Art, Minimalism and Conceptualism to more recent, postmodern trends.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Introduction to Contemporary Theory
courses.description: A basic beginning survey of contemporary art, film and media theory, focusing specifically on: realism, formalism, semiotics, phenomenology, psychoanalysis, feminism, Marxism, gender/queer studies, poststructuralism, post-colonial theory and broader issues of authorship, narratology, postmodernism, and multiculturalism.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Visual Arts as Culture
courses.description: Exploration of visual arts and culture, including the evolving social and practical parameters of technologically produced images and the shifting arenas of ideology, analysis, and criticism.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Digital Video
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units. Letter grade required for majors.
courses.description: The making and use of video in contemporary art. Hands-on production and post production are combined with viewing, critique, and discussion topics, including cultural prominence and future trends. Single and multiple channel, installation, and integration with other media are all encouraged.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Memory: An Interdisciplinary Exploration
courses.description: Introduces students to the trans-disciplinary fields of memory and migration through interdisciplinary collaboration. Course responsibilities include class participation, a midterm essay and a final interdisciplinary project. This course draws upon the connections between neuroscience, arts and studies of human migration.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Personal Narrative
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units.
courses.description: Intensive writing-based workshop designed for formulating and producing artwork based on one's own personal experiences and histories. Experimentation and expansion into other artistic media are encouraged.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Spoken Word
courses.description: A workshop introduction to the use of voice as an artistic medium, with emphasis on personal monologue, and improvisation.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Art and Science of Aerospace Culture
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units. Same course as Engineering 177 and MAT 258
courses.description: Interdisciplinary course/seminar/practice that explores technological, aesthetic, cultural, and political aspects of the space side of the aerospace complex. Design history,space complex aesthetics, cinema intersections, imaging/telecommunications, human spaceflight history, reduced/alternating gravity experimentation, space systems design/utilization.

courses.subject: ART
courses.title: Special Topics in Art
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 16 units.
courses.description: Special topics in art.

courses.subject: ART
