courses.description: Introduction to "pagan" spirituality: Rites marking the seasonal and life cycles, syncretism and multiculturalism, initiation into religious associations, dreams and oracles, with attention both to religious texts and to the symbolic, iconographic, and structural evidence offered by archaeological data.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: The Sacred Geography of the Ancient Mediterranean World
courses.description: A survey of religious sites in paganism, early Christianity, ancient Judaism, and early Islam. After general introduction to the sites, theoretical approaches to sacred space and ritual, and research methods for archaeological materials, students produce research papers and oral presentations on individual sites.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religions of the Ancient Near East
courses.description: Examination of the religious traditions of Mesopotamia, the Hittites, and the peoples of Syria-Palestine as seen through their literary archeological remains.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: The History of Anti-Semitism
courses.description: A systematic examination of the history of anti-Semitism, beginning with the emergence of anti-Judaism in the world of late antiquity, its transformation into theological anti-Semitism in the middle ages, and the emergence of racial anti-Semitism in the modern world. The central focus will be anti-Semitism as a religio-historical category.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Politics and Religion of Jerusalem
courses.prereq_text: Upper-division standing or a prior course in religious studies.
courses.description: This course surveys the religious, political, and cultural history of Jerusalem over three millennia as a symbolic focus of three faiths: Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. Course content focuses on the transformation of sacred space as reflected by literary and archaeological evidence by examining the testimony of artifacts, architecture, and iconography in relation to the written word.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Introduction to Rabbinic Literature
courses.description: An introduction to the basic texts of Rabbinic literature through an analysis of representative passages from the Mishnah, Talmud, and Midrash. Particular attention will be given to the various types of Midrash and the principles and methods of Midrashic interpretation. (Knowledge of Hebrew not required.)

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Holy Delight: Eros and the Sacred in Jewish and Christian Interpretations of the Song of Songs
courses.description: Explores the allegorical and symbolic interpretations of the biblical love poem known as the Song of Songs in the Jewish and Christian traditions from Late Antiquity to the Middle Ages. Topics to be discussed include the Song in its literary and historical context, the interplay of the sacred and the erotic in religious experience, allegory and the sacralization of the erotic, Marian interpretations and the ascetic curbing of desire, and the contemplative and ectastic interpretations of medieval kabbalists.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Jewish Dream Interpretation from the Bible to Freud
courses.description: Explores the varieties of dream interpretation in the Jewish tradition from the Bible to Freud. Topics to be discussed include dream and transcendence in the religious imagination and neuroscience; dreams and prophecy; the hermeneutics of dream interpretation; lucid dreaming and the syntax of space and time in the dream consciousness.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Jewish Law
courses.description: A survey of the development of Jewish Law from the times of the Bible, through the Dead Sea Scrolls, New Testament, Rabbinic Literature, and medieval literature. The main emphasis in this course will be the development of Jewish Law in Judaism throughout history, raising questions of continuity and change.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Identity, Feminism, and Secularism in Hebrew Literature
courses.comments: Comparative Literature 184C and Religious Studies 133E are the same course.
courses.description: Provides a broad overview of Modern Hebrew literature, spanning from its origins in the eighteenth century to the contemporary era. Aims to shed light on the factors that make this literature distinctive and fascinating. The course delves into various themes, such as Jewish identity, feminism, secularism, and Zionism, while examining the interplay and conflicts between different generations of literary works. The readings for the course comprise a selection of short stories in translation, but will be available in Hebrew for interested students. All lectures and discussions will be held in English.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Image of Jews in Film
courses.description: An introduction to the representation of Jews in film. Individual films are contextualized, followed by a discussion.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Readings in Tibetan Buddhist Texts
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit.
courses.description: Close readings of the different genres of the classical texts of Tibetan Buddhism in the original Tibetan: philosophy, history, autobiography, religious poetry, ritual, etc. Also provides a hands-on introduction to available digital tools.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Gnosticism and Manichaeism
courses.description: Study of Gnostic and Manichaean religions as philosophical and ritual systems, as book religions, and in their interrelations with Christianity, Judaism, Zoroastrianism, and Platonism.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Topics in Catholic Studies
courses.description: Various courses on the topic of Catholic Studies, including courses taught by the Tipton Visiting Professor in Catholic Studies.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Catholicism and Modernity
courses.description: An examination of key concepts in the history of Catholic thought: the sacred/sacraments, tradition, sacrifice, sex, and authority with attention to how these concepts were interpreted and reinterpreted by Catholic thinkers and scholars of religion in the modern era.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Islamic Traditions
courses.description: Introduction to history, doctrines, and practices of the Sunni, Shi'i and Sufi expressions of Islam. Includes study of Qur'an, Hadith literature, religious law, leadership, and holy places.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religion, Politics and Society in the Persian Gulf Region
courses.description: History of Islam and politics in societies of Saudia Arabia, Iran, and Iraqsince 1500. Emphasis on topics such as Shi'i and Sunni movements, religion and the state, Iranian revolution, economic development, and modernity.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Islamic Mysticism and Religious Thought
courses.description: Sufi mystics, ideas, practices, and movements. The relationship of Sufism to other currents of religious thought, such as theology and philosophy in the middle east, Africa, and Asia.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Islam in South Asia
courses.description: Examines the religious, cultural, social, and political formation of Islam in India, from the twelth century to the present. Special consideration is given to patterns of Islamization and Hindu-Muslim encounters in pilgrimage, mysticism, and music. Religious aspects of Indian nationalisticmovements and the 1947 partition are also discussed.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Islam in America
courses.comments: Same course as Black Studies 140E.
courses.description: Examines Islam in American setting, from introduction by African slaves and immigrants from Islamic countries, to transformation into the black Muslim movement, to rise as one of the leading non-Christian religions in the United States during the 1970s and 80s.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Sociology of Religion: The Classical Statements
courses.description: Religion as it is treated by major social theorists, including Marx, Weber,Durkheim, Freud, Simmel, Malinowski.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Church-State Relations
courses.description: Examines relationship between American government and religion with particular attention to Establishment Clause jurisprudence and interest group politics. Teaches analytical methods of reading case law and public interest litigation.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religious Liberty
courses.description: Examines commitments to religious freedom as an essential part of modern politics. Teaches analytical case law method to read U.S. cases as well as rulings of international courts protecting civil and human rights.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religious Literature in Hebrew
courses.description: Introduction to poetry of the Hebrew bible with special reference to Culticsongs. Texts will be selected from psalms, song of songs, and Koheleth in order to examine the varieties of poetic style.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: The Problem of Evil in Religious Traditions
courses.description: This course surveys key philosophical formulations and responses to the problem of evil, including natural evil (e.g. diseases) and moral evil (e.g. injustices), as expressed across religious traditions, including the Ancient Greeks, Judaism, Christianity and Islam. The focus of the course is a comparative reading of philosophical and religious primary sources in their historical and cultural contexts.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: ATHEISM
courses.description: Do atheists believe in anything? If so, what? Is a religious atheist an oxymoron?This course explores what atheism is and how its changed over time. It also introduces students to related forms of nonbelief, such as agnosticism, humanism, and freethought. By looking at the wide variety of atheisms, a fascinating story emerges about what it means to believe, behave, and belong in religious and nonreligious ways.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Patterns in Comparative Religion
courses.prereq_text: Upper division standing and one course on religion (lower or upper division).
courses.description: Study of major religious issues as addressed by more than one religious tradition. The problem of comparative religion as an academic discipline.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religion and the American Experience
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 8 units.
courses.description: Study of one selected topic in U.S. religious history in cultural context. Examples include evangelicalism, revivalism, fundamentalism, millennialism, communalism, Transcendentalism, new religions past and present, metaphysical traditions, religion and ethnicity, religion and healing, nature religion, New Age.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Introduction to Daoism
courses.comments: EACS 147T and RG ST 147T are the same course.
courses.description: A study of the classical sources of Daoism, followed by a consideration of the varieties of religious practice which developed from those sources.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Advanced Arabic
courses.description: Advanced study of grammar and vocabulary; readings in the major genres of classical and modern Arabic literature, including Qur'an, medieval poetry and prose, modern short story and novels, etc.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Advanced Arabic
courses.description: Continuation of Relgious Studies 148A.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Advanced Arabic
courses.description: Continuation of Relgious Studies 148B.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Reading and Translating Arabic
courses.description: Introduces Advanced Arabic Grammar and vocabulary with readings of Arabic literature from a variety of contexts, ranging from Medieval to Modern Arabic literatures and cultures, and is open to students of different backgrounds in Arabic, with minimum proficiency in two years of Arabic or their equivalent.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Islamic Humanism
courses.description: This course investigates humanist themes that were the product of the Arab-Islamic reception of Greek thought in the early and classical period of Islamic history (~800- 1258) as championed in the works of literators, philosophers, and historians. The objective of this course is to introduce these humanist themes through close reading and examination of primary sources in their historical, multicultural, and multi-religious contexts.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Islamic Philosophy and Theology
courses.description: This course surveys the history of rationalist thought in pre-modern Islamic history, focusing on the genesis and development of the disciplines of rationalist theology and Neoplatonized Aristotelian philosophy. The objective of this course is to highlight the experimental and dynamic scope of rationalist thought in pre-modern Islamic history through close reading of primary sources in their broader historical and intellectual contexts.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religion and Wrestling
courses.description: Explores the relationship between religion and professional wrestling in the twentieth century. Through analysis of historical case studies, wrestlers careers and gimmicks, promotions, news coverage, journals, scrapbooks, and fan culture, we interrogate this thesis: that wrestling is a site and species of religious ritual. In what ways is it right or wrong? In what ways can we challenge or re-describe its categories? Religion, ritual, play, embodiment, and popular culture will be the objects of our analysis in this course, and we will pursue new understandings of their convergence and co-dependency in modern American history.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religion in America Today
courses.description: Recent trends in American religion and in interrelationships between religion and American society.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religion and Technology
courses.description: This course helps students understand the complex relationship between religion and technology. Religions that reject technology are the exception rather than the rule. Christians have long used new media to reach potential converts, and new tech inspired the creation of religions like Spiritualism and Scientology. Many religious leaders adopted video streaming technology during the COVID-19 pandemic, and apps abound for reading scriptures, praying, and mindfulness meditation. Some versions of this course will be taught partially or entirely in virtual reality with the aid of VR headsets like the Oculus Quest 3, which UCSBs library holds in its reserves system.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Metaphysical Spirituality
courses.description: What do spiritual people believe and practice? What do astrology, Tarot, Theosophy, and Afro-futurism have in common? This course introduces students to the history and variety of the metaphysical tradition, which is often called spirituality in the U.S. and other parts of the world. Readings and lectures trace connections across different beliefs and practices to show how they share common roots, while also explaining why the metaphysical tradition is so eager to appropriate from non-western cultures. Students will learn to recognize a tradition that remains subterranean despite its broad and varied influence.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Bio-Medical Ethics
courses.description: Moral, social, and legal questions surrounding the practice of medicine and related sciences. Topics may include patient's rights, ethical duties of doctors, stem cell research, end of life care, and physician assisted suicide.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Seminar in Social Ethics
courses.prereq_text: Instructor approval required prior to enrolling.
courses.description: This seminar is part of the Capps Center internship program in public service and social ethics. It addresses issues of ethics and the role of governmental and non-governmental organizations in contemporary society. Students will intern in local non-profit organizations in Winter and Spring quarters.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Ethics and the College Experience
courses.comments: Students cannot enroll in this course if they have received credit for RGST 156DJ.
courses.description: Critical examination of moral, social and political issues that arise on college campuses. Examines theories and methods of reasoning about moral relations, rights, duties, dissent, and conflicts arising in the shared campus community. Explores the challenges and opportunities available to college students as learners, and raises questions about the role of the student and the purpose of the university as a whole.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Social Ethics Research
courses.description: Research paper part of the Capps Center internship program in public service and social ethics. It describes the student's experience working in a nonprofit organization, combining theoretical material from the previous course on social ethics in fall quarter and practical experience during the winter and spring quarters.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Environmental Ethics
courses.description: Environmental Ethics probes questions of duty and policy regarding human impact on the natural world. Topics such as climate change, sustainable economics, population explosion, and the standing of non-human animals are examined from various perspectives.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Contemporary Persian Literature and Translation
courses.prereq_text: RGST 57D or RGST 58B or Instructor Approval
courses.description: Introduces students to 20th century Persian-language literary texts as a means of understanding the efforts of an ever-expanding Iranian intellectual class over this period via use of both the short story and the novel. The course seeks to familiarize students whose command of Persian is at Intermediate or Advanced level. Students increase their fluency in reading and learn to exercise an enhanced facility in the language.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Persian Cinema
courses.prereq_text: RGST 57D or RGST 58B or Instructor Approval
courses.description: The study of Persian Movies. During this course, Persian language learners watch and analyze some creative Iranian movies, developing their language skills and learning about the Persian culture. Course objectives include developing vocabulary of daily language, comprehension and critical analysis of Persian movies, writing summaries of the movies, engaging with various aspects of Persian-speaking culture.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Persian Media and Translation
courses.prereq_text: RGST 57D or RGST 58B or Instructor Approval
courses.description: The study of authentic Persian news, reports, songs, and movies through a variety of media sources, such as print, radio, television, and internet. Course objectives include developing vocabulary and reading of news; reading, translating, and summarizing news reports; comprehension and critical analysis of Persian movies; reading and analysis of Persian ballads and songs; and engaging with various aspects of Persian-speaking culture.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Persian Translation
courses.prereq_text: RGST 57D or RGST 58B or Instructor Approval
courses.description: The course aims to develop skills in technologies of translation. The students learn about literal translation versus free translation. Students develop practical and research skills that are of immediate importance to the translation of different texts (i.e. articles, media, and short stories). Upon completion of this course, students should be able to formulate and employ appropriate translation strategies to overcome language and cultural barriers of different texts and translate with confidence from English to Persian and vice versa.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Classic Persian Literature and Translation
courses.prereq_text: RGST 57D or RGST 58B or Instructor Approval
courses.description: The aim of the course is for students to become acquainted with a number of representative works of Classical Persian literature and to identify enduring themes in the literature. Short poems and excerpts from long poems will be read and discussed in class. This course seeks to familiarize students whose command of Persian is at Advanced level. Students will increase their fluency in reading and learn to exercise an enhanced facility in the language.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Consciousness and the Body in Hindu Traditions
courses.description: An exploration of Hindu constructions of embodiment and the relationship of the mind-body complex to consciousness. Critical analysis of discursive representations and practices in various Hindu traditions, including ritual traditions, ascetic movements, legal codes, medical discourses, devotional movements, and Tantric traditions.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Intensive Advanced Persian I
courses.comments: No credit can be earned if more advanced credit in the language has already been awarded. Cannot be taken concurrently with Religious Studies 157A-B-C.
courses.description: A continuation of Intensive Intermediate Persian II (RGST 58D). The course objectives are: develop advanced language skills in listening, speaking, writing, and reading comprehension; practice reading and translating texts at an advanced level; communicate in Persian on a variety of topics; learn variety of real-life language tasks through writing paragraphs, short essays, reports, and summaries.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Intensive Advanced Persian II
courses.comments: No credit can be earned if more advanced credit in the language has already been awarded. Cannot be taken concurrently with RGST 157A-B-C. ��
courses.description: A continuation of Intensive Advanced Persian I (RGST 158E). The course objectives are: develop advanced language skills; initiate and carry complex conversations; practice reading and translating texts at an advanced level; write complex paragraphs; develop cultural awareness through additional readings, movies, and class discussions.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Elementary Sanskrit
courses.description: An introduction to the phonology, morphology, and syntax of classical Sanskrit.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Elementary Sanskrit
courses.description: Continuation of Elementary Sanskrit.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Elementary Sanskrit
courses.description: Reading and analysis of classical Sanskrit religious texts.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Intermediate Sanskrit
courses.description: Selected readings in intermediate level Sanskrit religious texts: Bhagavad-Gita

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Intermediate Sanskrit
courses.description: Selected readings in intermediate level Sanskrit religious texts: Upanishads

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Intermediate Sanskrit
courses.description: Selected readings in intermediate level Sanskrit religious texts: Epics

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religious Literature in Sanskrit
courses.description: Readings in religious literature in Sanskrit.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religious Literature in Sanskrit: Vedic Literature
courses.description: Readings in Vedic literature in Sanskrit.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religious Literature in Sanskrit: Mahabharata
courses.description: Readings in the Mahabharata in Sanskrit.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religious Literature in Sanskrit: Puranas
courses.description: Readings in the Puranas in Sanskrit.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religious Literature in Sanskrit: Yoga Literature
courses.description: Readings in Yoga literature in Sanskrit.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religious Literature in Sanskrit: Philosophical Literature
courses.description: Readings in Philosophical literature in Sanskrit.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religious Literature in Sanskrit: Tantric Literature
courses.description: Readings in Tantric literature in Sanskrit.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religious Literature in Sanskrit: Buddhist Literature
courses.description: Readings in Buddhist literature in Sanskrit.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religious Literature in Sanskrit: Jain Literature
courses.description: Readings in Jain literature in Sanskrit.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religious Traditions of India
courses.comments: Not open for credit to students who have completed Religious Studies 160.
courses.description: An introduction to the classical religious traditions of India, with particular attention to three major areas of Indian religion and culture: the ritual, moral and social order; philosophical perspectives and traditions; and traditions of mythology and devotion.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Indian Philosophy
courses.description: An overview of the six classical philosophical schools (darshanas) of Hinduism. May also include analysis of selected portions of the Jain and Buddhist philosophical traditions.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Introduction to Jainism
courses.description: Focuses on the Jain tradition with its historical roots in South Asia. Surveys the sacred writings, beliefs, religious figures, and practices integral to the Jain tradition from the time of Mahavira (fifth century B.C.E.) to the present day.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Desire, Sex, and Romance in Traditions of India
courses.prereq_text: Upper Division standing and one course from the following: RGST 19, 20, 140D, 158C, 159 G-H-J-K-L-M-N-O, 160 A, 161D, 169 or equivalent; or Instructor approval.
courses.comments: Cross listed with C LIT 162I
courses.description: Explores questions of love and sex across two thousand years of Indian religious thought. The reading list includes some of the most famous voices in South Asian literary history. We will tour various genres: moral teachings, epic narrative, drama, devotional and mystical poetry, modern fiction. Yes, we will read the Kama Sutra, and yes, there will be Bollywood films.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Many Ramayanas: Ancient and Modern
courses.comments: Some prior study of South Asian Religions suggested.
courses.description: India’s Ramayana is a rip-roaring adventure story, with kings, queens, heroes, villains, lovers, monsters, magic, and miracles. Over thousands of years across South Asia, it has also been the master narrative defining issues of critical ideological importance: power, gender, race, caste, divinity, dharma. In this course we study the canonical Sanskrit text in translation and sample some of the epic’s tellings in vernacular media, including comic books, live performance, and television. The emphasis, however, will be on cinema, with a lineup of films featuring several spectacular recent Bollywood productions. How does this story, popular for more than two thousand years, speak to the politics of the present?

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Topics in Buddhist Studies
courses.description: Various courses on the topic of Buddhist Studies

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Race and Religion in the American West
courses.description: Examines the role of race, religion, and region within a history of encounters that influenced the construction and development of the American West from the 19th century to the present. Topics explored can include how the convergence of different racial and religious groups transformed ideas related to race and ethnicity, transnationalism, the environment and technology, new religious traditions, and broader conceptions of American religious history.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religion in Japanese Culture
courses.comments: Japan 167A and Religious Studies 167A are the same course.
courses.description: A historical analysis of the major components of the classical and medieval religious systems of Japan, through investigation of texts, rituals, and institutions.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Shinto through the Ages
courses.comments: RG ST175B and JAPAN 175B are the same course.
courses.description: Explores the diversity of the Shinto tradition through an analysis of representative original texts in English translation ranging from ancient mythology (Kojiki, Nihon shoki, and Fudoki) and medieval syncretic discourses, to modern forms of Shinto nationalism.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Buddhist Political Thought and Institutions
courses.comments: EACS 176 and RG ST 176 are the same course.
courses.description: Buddhist political theories and practices in various Asian countries from antiquity to the present, with special emphasis on ideas of kinship and republicanism, state-formation process, cultural identity, and the interactions with other religions.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Visual Culture of Buddhism
courses.comments: EACS 179 and Religious Studies 179 are the same course.
courses.description: This course explores the rich world of Buddhist visual culture, ranging from meditation to addressing the use of painted images in public performances. It focuses on sacred images, their rituals, and theories of representation behind their creation and use.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Mysticism
courses.comments: Not open for credit to students who have completed German 169. Same course as Comparative Literature 179B and German 179B.
courses.description: Analysis of German mystical writing, its roots in ancient Greek texts, revolutionary impact, links with other mystical traditions, and influence on secular literature. Texts include Hildegard von Bingen, Meister Eckhart, Mechthild von Magdeburg, Novalis, Rilke, etc. Taught in English.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Shi'ism Before and After the Iranian Revolution
courses.description: An examination of a century of evolution of Iranian Shi'ism. Readings include: Early 20th century secular Iranian thinkers who formulated a new discourse on rationalist Shi'ism; the mid-twentieth-century lay writers and religious thinkers moved to a more militant discourse of Islamism; and a generation of clerics and theologians who have articulated a more tolerant and hermeneutic interpretation of Shi'ism in the last two decades in an attempt to reconcile Shi'i doctrines with social and economic modernities.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religious Practice and the State in China
courses.comments: Same course as Chinese 183B.
courses.description: Historical and anthropological approaches to the interaction between religious practice and state forces, with emphasis on popular religion and the decline and revival of religion in Chinese modernity.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Tibetan Buddhist Literature
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 12 units, but only 4 units may be used towards the major.
courses.description: A thematic and text-centered investigation of an aspect of the Tibetan Buddhist religious/philosophical tradition. In any given year, focuses on a genre of the Tibetan religious/literary corpus; e.g., biography and the "stages of the path," "great perfection," or Tantric literature.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Food, Religion, and Culture in the Middle East
courses.prereq_text: A previous course in Global Studies, Religious Studies, History, Anthropology, or Sociology; upper-division standing.
courses.description: Explores the significance of foods in the religious and cultural life of Middle Eastern peoples. Using primary and secondary resources, takes a historical approach to the culinary cultures of Muslims, Christians and Jews, including feasting, fasting, and dietary rules. Includes critical examination of how Arab, Persian, Turkish, and Jewish ethnic communities establish identities and relationships through culinary practices. Food sovereignty, sustainability, and social resilience in the face of adversity are also examined in different contexts.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Politics of Veiling in Modern Egypt
courses.description: Examines the contemporary religious politics of love, sex and gender relations in Egypt. As in the United States, the proper organization of intimate life and women's bodies has been placed at the center of politics. Politics has become intensely personal, joining political projects of religious nation-making with personal decisions as to how people, and particularly young women, should organize their private lives and navigate the public sphere.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Seminar in Civic Engagement and Deliberative Democracy
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 8 units.
courses.description: This three-quarter-long course is part of the Civic Engagement Scholars Program. In the Fall, students study theoretical framework and historical background of civic engagement in the American university. Students engage in leadership development and learn practices that leaders use to transform values into actions, visions into realities, obstacles into innovations, and risks into rewards. Students develop and practice skills for deliberative discourse, including how to have civil conversations on controversial topics. Students design workshops on a topic of their interest incorporating these issues and skills. In the Winter and Spring, they deliver these workshops to student organizations and the community.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Seminar in Civic Engagement and Deliberative Democracy
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 4 units.
courses.description: This three-quarter-long course is part of the Civic Engagement Scholars Program. In the Fall, students study theoretical framework and historical background of civic engagement in the American university. Students engage in leadership development and learn practices that leaders use to transform values into actions, visions into realities, obstacles into innovations, and risks into rewards. Students develop and practice skills for deliberative discourse, including how to have civil conversations on controversial topics. Students design workshops on a topic of their interest incorporating these issues and skills. In the Winter and Spring, they deliver these workshops to student organizations and the community.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Seminar in Civic Engagement and Deliberative Democracy
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 4 units.
courses.description: This three-quarter-long course is part of the Civic Engagement Scholars Program. In the Fall, students study theoretical framework and historical background of civic engagement in the American university. Students engage in leadership development and learn practices that leaders use to transform values into actions, visions into realities, obstacles into innovations, and risks into rewards. Students develop and practice skills for deliberative discourse, including how to have civil conversations on controversial topics. Students design workshops on a topic of their interest incorporating these issues and skills. In the Winter and Spring, they deliver these workshops to student organizations and the community.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Topics in Religious Studies
courses.description: Features lectures by various visiting professors or adjunct lecturers on topics pertaining to the study of religions using various methodological approaches to subjects thatare the specialty of the respective instructors. Course content will vary.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Spirituality of the Beats
courses.description: An exploration of the cross-cultural religious sources influencing major American poets associated with the Beat movement, such as Allen Ginsberg, Anne Waldman, or Amiri Baraka. Students will have the option of a research-driven or creative final project.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Ethical Investing to Impact Social Change
courses.description: What are corporate Americas ethical responsibilities to its constituents? This discussion-based course explores Conscience investing i.e. directing investments to address ESG (i.e. Environmental, Societal and Corporate Governance) challenges. Topics include: What is Socially Responsible Investing and how does it differ from Impact Investing? How can investments help address poverty, global health, climate change? How can students hone their presentation skills to engage and persuade more effectively? Students can enhance their personal financial skills as they gain how-to real-life perspectives on leading ESG challenges and investment best-practices.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: First Contact
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 8 units.
courses.description: A humanities-based interdisciplinary course on the problems and issues of first contact and interactions between humanity and non-Terran entities. What do the histories, experiences, and interactions of humans with other humans, animals, plants, AIs and postulated superhuman beings reveal about our limitations, biases and opportunities in the preparations for first contact? How might the humanities (religious studies, literature, history, philosophy, ethics, etc.) contribute to the protocols and thinking about first contact that move beyond scientific, pragmatic and anthropocentric western paradigms of rational knowledge and subjectivity.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: The Fatigue is the Sharia: Old and New Debates
courses.description: Discusses old and new debates on the viability, illness, and death of the Shari'a. The Shari'a is broadly understood as the laws of Islam, though this concept is fine tuned considerably in the course of our discussions. The course places on a continuum two kinds of debates: debates in the Islamic tradition about the end of access to divine guidance and debates in modern scholarship in Islamic legal studies about the end of the Shari'a. The resulting continuum covers what access to divine guidance means and how it relates to Shari'a.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Have Ethics Gone Awry? A Contrast of Then and Now
courses.description: Ever wonder how we got to now? Many socio-economic challenges are traceable to the Gilded Age (1865-1900) when the U.S. grew from a fledging agrarian society to a major industrial power. This discussion-based course balances theory with application to explore:-Whether those gains were worth the costs?-Were Divine Providence and Manifest Destiny doctrines misused to exploit immigrants, workers, indigenous and people of color?-Were the renown industrialists who built this nation actually Robber Barons?-How can students hone their presentation skills to more effectively engage and persuade?Join us as this course may change your perspective forever!

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Studies of Non-Violence
courses.description: The doctrine of nonviolence is applicable across South Asian Religious Traditions. Students will be introduced to the background of nonviolence and its contemporary expressions. This course is divided into two main parts: theoretical aspects of nonviolence and how nonviolence is applied across cultures to problems of the environment and social justice. Practical aspects of nonviolence will merge philosophies of East and West, explaining nonviolence in daily lives.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Mission Santa Barbara: History and Society
courses.description: This course examines the art, architecture, and history of Mission Santa Barbara, with an emphasis on using primary sources (written, visual, and archaeological) to understand different ways in which a religious institution and civic community can interact.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Intermediate Vietnamese Language
courses.description: Exposes students to more advanced vocabulary, grammatical forms, and linguistic structures. Students will practice reading and conversation to a more advanced level, by being exposed to short stories, videos, films, and more complex conversational situations.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Intermediate Vietnamese Language II
courses.description: Continuation of Int Vietnamese I

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Intermediate Vietnamese Language III
courses.description: Continuation of Vietnamese II

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Wall Street Ethics and Economic Calamities
courses.description: What is a governments economic responsibility to its citizens as they pursue happiness and prosperity? This discussion-based course balances theory with real-life case studies to explore:-What are business cycles and monetary/fiscal policy responses to them during historys most prominent financial crises?-How does money and banking move our economy?-What ethical misdeeds have contributed to financial downturns?-How can students hone their presentation skills to engage and persuade more effectively?Students can enhance their personal financial skills as they gain a historical context lessons learned that can model ethically considerate behavior in their own lives.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Latino Religious Thought
courses.description: Examination of the indigenous, Iberian and North American sources and influences for distinctly Latino forms of religious thought, speculation, and spiritual construction. Topics include: Nahua wisdom traditions, colonial Nepantla, Chicano movement indigenismo, feminist innovation, Latino liberationist theology.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religion and Healing in Global Perspective
courses.description: Comparative and cross-cultural introduction to relationships between religion, science, and healing arts, using selected case studies and stressing alternatives to mainstream western medicine. Attention to underlying religio-philosophical worldviews and to the ways in which they influence healing practices.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Senior Honors Thesis
courses.prereq_text: Two prior upper-division courses in religious studies; consent of instructoand department; senior standing; open to religious studies majors only.
courses.description: Projects for advanced work in Religious Studies in conjunction with individual members of the faculty and developed by students. For honors students who with to graduate with the distinction in Religious Studies.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Internship
courses.description: These internships allow students to collaborate with philanthropic and non-profit organizations, nationally and globally. Working digitally or on site with the organization, students learn about practical implications of a degree in Religious Studies and in the Humanities more generally. They also have the opportunity to utilize their knowledge of foreign languages and technology. While helping to make the world a better place, students gain valuable experience that can be applied to their chosen career after graduation.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Iranian Studies Digital Internship
courses.description: Sit in your room and make the world a better place! Digital internships connect you to non-profit organizations (NGOs). Work from home six hours a week and attend one workshop during the quarter. Internships might include the following: create and run a new non-profit; create a new website for an NGO; raise funds for the education of youth; learn and contribute to effective parenting techniques; work with the International Book Fund and help build a village library; document the therapeutic effects of arts for those who suffer from PTSD; become the English-language editor of a journal; work with centers that help individuals displaced by war, environmental disasters, economic disadvantages, and intolerance; work with UNICEF.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Independent Studies in Religion
courses.prereq_text: Two upper-division courses in religious studies; consent of instructor and department
courses.comments: Students must have a minimum 3.0 GPA for the preceeding 3 quarters and are limited to 5 units per quarter and 30 units total in all 98/99/198/199/199AA-ZZ courses combined.
courses.description: Projects for work in religious studies in conjunction with individual members of the faculty and developed by students.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Persian Language Independent Study
courses.comments: Students must have a minimum 3.0 GPA for the preceeding 3 quarters and are limited to 5 units per quarter and 30 units total in all 98/99/198/199/199AA-ZZ courses combined.
courses.description: Independent study in Persian language in conjunction with the Persian instructor.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Independent Research Assistance
courses.prereq_text: Two upper-division courses in religious studies; consent of instructor and department
courses.comments: Students must have a minimum 3.0 GPA for the preceeding 3 quarters and are limited to 5 units per quarter and 30 units total in all 98/99/198/199/199AA-ZZ courses combined.
courses.description: Faculty supervised reseach. Written work is usually required.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Core Concepts in Religious Studies
courses.description: Seminar focuses on core concepts in the study of religion and meets a 200 Course requirement for the MA-Plan2, MA/PhD, or PhD tracks in Religious Studies. Course topics will vary.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: After the Human
courses.description: Special seminar taught by philosopher Mark C. Taylor. As the Anthropocene heats up, the possibility of human extinction grows. Today’s most pressing problems are not only scientific, technological, political, and economic, but also philosophical and spiritual. The foundation of the Anthropocene is the anthropocentric metaphysics that begins with Descartes and ends with Nietzsche. We will examine an alternative vision: the structural and operational logic of the coemergent and codependent webs that comprise our world, from the quantum and biochemical through bodily and ecological systems to plant, animal, human and “artificial” intelligence. What comes after the human? What might all of this have to do with what once was called God?

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Proseminar in History and Theory of Religion
courses.description: Critical analysis of the key themes and figures in modern philosphy and psychology of religion, with attention to their role in the emergence and current practice of religious studies. Includes the works of such figures as Spinoza, Hume, Kant, Hegel, Marx, Nietzsche, Heidegger, Wittgenstein, Freud, and Jung.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religion and the Body
courses.description: The seminar explores the contributions of scholarship on the body in religion to re-visioning theories of the body from the methodological perspective of the history of religions. We will examine three areas of scholarship that have had a significant influence on contemporary theories: the body in philosophy, the body in social theory, and the body in feminist and gender studies. We will critically interrogate the limitations of these Western theoretical models through an analysis of categories and models of the body that are grounded in the distinctive idioms of non-Western religious traditions, with a focus on six modalities: ritual bodies, ascetic bodies, gendered bodies, sexual bodies, tantric bodies, and devotional bodies.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religion & Image
courses.description: Icons. idols, visions: In many cases, across traditions, images give form to Religious Experience. Questions of visual representation and recognition are central to religious studies. This proseminar will ground students in core texts that theorize visual forms and artifacts in religious life ad related fields of social practice. We will study historical and contemporary contributions from aesthetics, psychoanalysis, and semiotics, alongside other approaches that have shaped the course of inquiry in art history, film studies and anthropology. The syllabus will also highlight visual relations as prescribed and debated within cultic contexts, most notably among Christians and Hindus.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Phenomenology of Love
courses.description: In light of debate about the presence or absence of love in Martin Heidegger's thought, this course focuses on Heidegger's atheist inheritance of the theological analyses of love developed in Saint Augustine of Hippo. In and through this focus on the influence of a major theologian from late Antiquity in one of late-modernity's single most influential philosophers (decisive to phenomenology, hermeneutics, deconstruction, and Foucauldian genealogical thought, among others) the course serves as an introduction to twentieth-century Continental philosophy that highlights not only that philosophy's relevance to the study of religion but also the relevance of religion to engagement with such philosophy.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religion and Materiality
courses.description: An overview of various approaches to understanding materiality in the context of religion and of human culture generally, including concepts of landscape and taskscape, object agency, the new materialism, and material culture as archive. Attention is devoted to issues of equitable representation, colonialism and its effects, and ethical practices for the retrieval, possession, curation, and presentation of cultural objects.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religion & Nature
courses.description: This course critically examines the roles played by "religion" and "nature," within the context of North American cultural and environmental history. It will examine the contested ways in which religion and nature are understood, drawing on diverse sources and methodologies, and primary texts written by central figures in the field, both past and present. Specific topics include the origin and evolution of nature-religions and nature spirituality, religious naturalism, "greening of religions," and resistance to nature-inspired environmentalism. Students will gain a broad acquaintance with theoretical foundations, pivotal figures, social movements, etc.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religion & Politics
courses.description: This seminar adopts a history of longue durée to examine the mutual embeddedness of religion, politics, and the state across archaic, medieval, and modern social formations across the globe. It combines theoretical writings (Lefebvre, Foucault, Rappaport, Mahmood, Taylor, Lefort, Deleuze, and Guattari) with empirical analyses of religious politics in archaic states (Angkor, Inca, China, Aztecs, and Abrahamic religions). It explores religious movements in modernity in Korea, China, Mexico, Russia, India, and the US. Themes include ritualization of politics and states, gender politics, millenarianism, spatialization, "political theology," biopolitics, etc.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religion and Environment
courses.description: This seminar confronts the oppositions that helped launch modernity and the Anthropocene: Nature vs. Culture, and Religion vs. Science. Readings explore (re-)constructing, reconciling, and hybridizing religious environmentalisms in dialogue with modern science for our multispecies planetary flourishing. Issues and topics include: Anthropocene and Capitalocene; religious ontologies and environmental ethics; modern mechanistic science and an inert non-agential nature; human-animal-deity relationships; new animism; Gaia Theory; deep time; Asian religions as contrasted with Abrahamic religion. Theorists include Donna Haraway, Arne Naess, Bruno Latour, Philippe Descole, Viveiros de Castro.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Race & Religion
courses.description: This seminar interrogates the concept of "race" as an essential category of analysis for the study of religion. The genealogy of "race" as co-constitutive with "religion" in the west is considered. The course also examines adjacent concepts marking perceived bodily differences and hierarchical social arrangements including "ethnicity," and "caste," as well as linked forms of identity (class, sex, gender). The course includes discussions of how race continues to inform and influence the profession.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Ritual
courses.description: “Ritual” has a strong method and theory component and situated in a comparative frame of diverse case studies. Due to ritual’s broad relevance across traditions, this course is accessible to and instructive for all graduate students in our program. Focusing on ritual and theories thereof enables students to grapple in historically- and culturally-situated ways with important questions about the nature of religious life and sociality generally. Considers several recent ethnographic examples to illustrate many of the conceptual issues opened up by the category. Covers a range of classical and contemporary theories of ritual. The class culminates in research papers and presentations by students.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Secularism
courses.description: Surveys the 21st-century debates over secularism and locates them within a longer history of advocacy and critique. Students learn to distinguish among the various meanings of secularism and the secular, such as the separation of church and state, a philosophy with a this-worldly focus, religion-making, and the absence of religion. Students also consider whether secularism should continue to be a logic of governance, or if the contemporary critique of secularism has rendered it obsolete.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Spirituality
courses.description: Explores the history and variety of the metaphysical tradition, which is often called "spirituality" in the U.S. and other parts of the world. Though this tradition can stand alone, it often blends with established religions and is sometimes lumped with nonreligion. Readings are primary sources, and they reflect the tradition's diversity. The range of sources shows that metaphysical spirituality's various manifestations share common roots and reflects metaphysical eagerness to appropriate from non-western cultures. Students will learn to recognize a tradition that remains subterranean despite its broad and varied influence.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religion and Time
courses.description: Explores the phenomenology of the lived experience of time as it has been mediated by various religious cultures. Topics to be discussed include myths of creation and the engendering of the cosmological time of the past; revelation as the diremptive disruption of the present; messianic eschatology and the redemptive narrativization of the linear circularity of the future; ritualization of time and the cultivation of individual and communal memory; the interface between holy and mundane in the theo-politicization of space and time; the dialectical sense of the profane.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Tradition
courses.description: Centering the category tradition, students theorize ways the concept has been announced and enacted in three overlapping spheres: religious contexts, academic debates, and law. We engage classical theories of continuity and change, recent theorizations of invention, articulation, discursive tradition, and contemporary examples of scholars and activists reclaiming the category. Adjacent conceptual terrain to be covered includes discourses of orthodoxy and authenticity. The course is driven in part by examples from students research areas (e.g., ancestral invocations or the asserted status of sacred texts) in the service of our shared project to theorize claim-making about the standing of the past in the present.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Core Issues in the Study of Religion
courses.description: Introduces graduate students to core issues in modern studies of religions and other world views.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Muslim Diasporas and Law
courses.prereq_text: Graduate standing or professor approval. Graduate students will have additional readings and extra meetings with professor.
courses.description: Examines the legal and social issues raised by the presence of Muslims in contemporary Western Europe and the United States. Civil rights, accommodation, and the construction of a dichotomy between moderate Islam and Islamism will be discussed.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Anthropology of Religion and Modernity
courses.description: Survey of major works in the anthropology of religion, including Turner, Geertz, Comaroffs, Rappaport, Asad, Mahmood, Taussig, etc. Topics include nationalism, the state, gender, sexuality, colonialism, pilgrimage, ritual, media, globalization, conversion, and the public sphere. Ethnographies of diverse religious cultures are also included.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Seminar on Vedic Traditions
courses.description: A study of the sociocultural, mythological, and ritual traditions of Vedic India. Includes an exploration of the Indo-Aryan debate concerning Vedic origins, the canonical authority of Veda, cosmogonic and cosmological speculations, sociocultural taxonomies, and theories of Vedic ritual.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Seminar on Bhakti Traditions
courses.description: A study of medieval bhakti traditions in India, including an examination of the devotional schools and poet-saints of Saiva, Vaisnava, and Sakta traditions as well as devotional movements in Islamic and Sikh traditions.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Seminar on Philosophical Traditions of South Asia
courses.description: An examination of selected topics in South Asian philosophical traditions, including consideration of the six classical Hindu philosophical schools (Darsanas) as well as Jain and Buddhist philosophical traditions.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Seminar on Contemporary Issues in South Asian Religions
courses.comments: Course content variable. May be repeated for credit.
courses.description: Analyses of selected topics concerning contemporary South Asian religions. Possible topics include issues in post-colonial studies, religious nationalisms, responses to globalization, diaspora and the homeland, constructions of gender, and vernacular traditions.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Seminar on Subaltern Traditions and Counter-Traditions in South Asia
courses.comments: Please note that this new course is offered as an addition to the RG ST 206 series of core seminars within the graduate program in South Asian religions.
courses.description: Core seminar in South Asian Religions that covers religion as conceived, argued, and practiced by members of non-elite communities, in particular communities historically marginalized in Brahminical discourses. Primarily organized around debates in social theory, the reading list builds on some of the landmark works of the Subaltern Studies collective and moves on to consider recent ethnographic work on religious life in Dalit and Adivasi communities. What is a tradition, anyway? What does caste mean? Is subaltern still a useful analytic category?

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Death and Rebirth in Buddhist Medicine
courses.description: This course examines various canonical texts and medical treatises dealing with the conceptions of disease, death, and rebirth as well as therapeutics in South Asian and Tibetan Buddhist traditions.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religion and the Senses: Affect, Embodiment, Materiality
courses.description: Our objective is to (re-)materialize religion by focusing on things and feelings. We approach the religious sensorium as made up not only of sight, scent, sound, taste, and touch, but also emotions,sentiments, and intensities of affect. We consider the bodies formed by religious disciplines and technologies, through contact with thestuff (objects, spaces, and media) of everyday ritual practice and performance. Readings survey contemporary theoretical and social scientific scholarship on religious perception, sensation, and subjectivity. We examine the mind-body problem; the construction of sensory categories; and the influence of sensory hierarchies onformations of race/ethnicity, gender/sexuality, and class in religious contexts.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Seminar on Hindus and Muslims in South Asia
courses.description: An inquiry into the interaction of Hindus and Muslims in South Asian history and cultures. Topics include religious beliefs and rituals, social and political issues, mystical traditions, science and medicine, music, art, and literature.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religion and Ethnography: Theory, Praxis, Experience
courses.description: An introduction to the social scientific study of religion through the lens of the ethnographic method. Attends both to practical questions concerning the performance of qualitative research and to ethnography as a literary genre that captures the complexities of lived experience. Reading assignments may be divided into three categories: historical investigations of ethnographic theory and fieldwork praxis; close examinations of discrete religious sites; and interdisciplinary meditations on such themes as interpretation, ethics, authority, and cultural translation.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Mongolian Buddhism
courses.description: This seminar focuses on the history of Buddhism among different Mongolian ethnic groups, the important Mongolian Buddhist thinkers and their writings, and Buddhist institutions. The seminar examines the given topics by utilizing the historical, ethnographic, and literary sources.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Seminar on South Asian Buddhist Traditions
courses.description: Historical, textual, and critical analyses of selected topics in Buddhist traditions of South Asia.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Archaelogy and the Study of Religion
courses.prereq_text: An upper-division course in religious studies.
courses.description: An examination of the uses of archaeological materials to reconstruct the history of religions in the ancient world, with special attention to the relationships between material culture, religious iconography, epigraphy, and sacred texts.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religion and Politics in Modern Iran
courses.description: Readings will include key texts by contemporary scholars of Iran-- historians, political scientists, theologians, sociologists, and anthropologists-- who have examined the relation between religion and politics in modern Iran from the late 19th century to the present time.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religion and the Question of Subjectivity in Contemporary European Thought
courses.description: Exploration of critical responses within contemporary European thought to modern conceptions of subjectivity (from Luther and Descartes through Hegel and Nietzsche). Writers may include Husserl, Heidegger, Levinas, Derrida, and Marion.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religious Environmentalism in the Anthropocene
courses.description: What can ancient religious traditions do for environmental protection? This class examines doctrinal potentials andactual examples of religious environmentalism in China, India, Japan, and the U.S.: with Buddhism, Daoism,Hinduism, Shinto, and Protestantism.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Mysticism and Apophasis in Meister Eckhart, Heidegger, and Derrida
courses.description: Explores the apophatic nature of the mystical experience through an in-depth study of Meister Eckhart's Latin commentaries and German sermons. The primary focus will be on Eckhart but attention will be paid as well to the interpretation of his thought in Heidegger and Derrida.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Seminar in Catholic Studies
courses.description: An examination of selected topics in Catholic Studies with particular attention to theory and methods that relate the study of Catholicism to larger questions in religious studies, American history, and global studies.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Seminar on Religion, Politics & Society in the Persian Gulf
courses.prereq_text: Graduate standing. Graduate students will have extra readings and meetings, longer papers, and weekly presentations.
courses.description: Examines the dynamics of religion, politics, and society among countries in the Persian Gulf. The focus will be on Saudi Arabia, Iraq, and Iran, which will be placed in comparative perspective. Topics include Sunni-Shi'i relations, religion and modernity, religio-political movements, gender dynamics, and regional conflicts.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Islamic Mysticism and Religious Thought
courses.description: Sufi mystics, ideas, practices, and movements. The relationship of Sufism to other currents of religious thought, such as theology and philosophy in the middle east, Africa, and Asia.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Islam in America
courses.prereq_text: Graduate standing or professor approval. Graduate students will have additional readings and extra meetings with professor.
courses.description: Examines Islam in United States, from introduction by African American slaves and immigrants to the transformation into the black Muslim movement, to its rise as one of the leading non-Christian religions in the United States during the late 20th to early 21st century.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Church-State Relations
courses.prereq_text: Graduate standing or professor approval. Graduate students will have additional readings and extra meetings with professor.
courses.description: Examines relationship between American government and religion with particular attention to Establishment Clause jurisprudence and interest group policies. Teaches analytical methods of reading case law and public interest litigation. Concurrent with 141D.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religious Liberty
courses.prereq_text: Graduate standing or professor approval. Graduate students will have additional readings and extra meetings with professor.
courses.description: Examines commitments to religious freedom as an essential part of modern politics. Teaches analytical case law method to read U.S. cases and international court rulings protecting civil and human rights.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religion in American History to 1865
courses.description: Principal figures, groups, trends, and issues in religion in American history and culture to 1865.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Religion in American History Since 1865
courses.description: Principal figures, groups, trends, and issues in religion in America since 1865.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Seminar in Buddhist Studies
courses.comments: Topics vary; may be repeated for credit.
courses.description: Historical, philosophical, methodological, and/or bibliographical analysis of different aspects of Buddhism or of selected areas in the study of Buddhism.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Seminar in Religion in America
courses.comments: May be repeated.
courses.description: Examination of selected topics in American religion to investigate its basic religious structures and to explore the relationship of religious phenomena to their cultural context. Course content variable.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Readings in Taoism
courses.comments: Same course as CHIN 260.
courses.description: Selected readings from important Taoist texts. Depending on the year, primary sources will be read in original Chinese or in translation.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Graduate Seminar in Shinto Studies
courses.description: This seminar addresses various issues in Shinto studies, including the history of Shinto, Western perceptions of Shinto, Shinto art and theories of the representation of the sacred, and features of Shinto Nativism.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Readings in Chinese Buddhism
courses.comments: Same course as CHIN 266F.
courses.description: Selected readings in important Buddhist texts which were either originally written in Chinese or translated into that language. Depending on the year, primary sources will be read in original Chinese or in translation.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Carnival and the Carnivalesque
courses.comments: All Masters and doctoral students in Religious Studies, History and related fields are encouraged to enroll.
courses.description: The world turned upside down! This graduate seminar focuses on the carnivalesque as an analytic concept as well as on carnival as social practice in a comparative frame. We read ethnographic and historical studies of diverse junctures where radical play comes together with social change: rituals of social inversion, revolutionary performances, millenarian social movements, charivari, drag balls. Brazil, India, Haiti, England, France, Japan; Nietzsche, Bakhtin, Emma Goldman.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Method in Islamic Studies
courses.description: This course aims to train graduate students to approach current studies of Islam and Muslim societies, past and present, with a critical eye -- ultimately in order to prepare them to think of dissertation topics in Islamic studies.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Methods in the Study of Religion
courses.description: Teaches graduate students empirical methods in the study of religion, including archival research, fieldwork, interviewing, and quantitative analysis. Students read examples that employ these methods, learn the fundamentals of research design, conduct their own research, and develop research proposals they can use for a prospectus or funding proposal.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Fatawa Literature
courses.comments: Non-Islamicists are advised to consult the instructor.
courses.description: Investigates the responses of Muslim jurists to queries about practical matters (fatawa). Trains students to identify the legal arguments and techniques, both textual (Qur'an/Sunna) and extra-textual.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Apostasy and Heresy in Islam
courses.description: The vague line between heresy and apostasy has been kept unadjudicated by jurists. This course delves into the complexities of the issues of heresy and apostasy that interest students of Islamic law and philosophy and of Islamic history in general.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Guided Readings in Modern Arabic Literature
courses.description: Critical readings from a selection of 19th-20th-century works in Arabic, including autobiographies, novels, short stories, and poems from the Arab world. Readings focus on issues central to modern Arab society.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.description: Seminar in special areas of interest in religious studies. Specific course titles and topics to be announced by the department each quarter offered. Course content will vary.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Materiality
courses.description: An overview of various approaches to understanding materiality in the context of religion and of human culture generally, including cognitive archaeology, external symbolic storage, post-processual theory, constructions of memory, thing theory, and the concept of object agency.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Special Topics
courses.description: Seminar in special areas of interest in religious studies. Specific course titles and topics to be announced by the department each quarter offered. Course content will vary.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Internship
courses.description: These internships allow students to collaborate with philanthropic and non-profit organizations, nationally and globally. Working digitally or on site with the organization, students learn about practical implications of a degree in Religious Studies and in the Humanities more generally. They also have the opportunity to utilize their knowledge of foreign languages and technology. While helping to make the world a better place, students gain valuable experience that can be applied to their chosen career after graduation.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: T.A. and Associate Training Program.
courses.comments: May be repeated. No unit credit allowed toward advanced degree.
courses.description: Required orientation and on-the-job_instructors of teaching assistants and associates through consultations with_instructors, evaluation of their teaching through videotapes or other means of observation, follow-up consultations, teaching evaluation.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Directed Reading
courses.comments: Course content variable. May be repeated.
courses.description: Special readings selected under guidance of individual instructor to help the student make up particular gaps in his/her intellectual background thatare pertinent to his/her graduate program.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Directed Reading and Research
courses.description: Research and preparation of dissertation.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Individual Study for Master's or Ph.D. Examination for Advancement to Candidacy.
courses.comments: No unit credit allowed toward advanced degree.
courses.description: Individual study for Master's or Ph.D. examinations for advancement to candidacy.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Master's Project Research and Preparation
courses.description: For research underlying the project; writing the project.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Master's Project Research and Preparation
courses.description: For research underlying the project; writing the project.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Ph.D. Dissertation Preparation
courses.description: Terminal preparation of the dissertation.

courses.subject: RG ST
courses.title: Ph.D. Dissertation Preparation
courses.description: Terminal preparation of the dissertation.

courses.description: Comprehensive introduction to Russian. Focus on developing basic communicative skills (speaking, listening comprehension, reading, writing) within the framework of contemporary Russian culture. Students acquire a basic grammatical framework for further language study. Audio, visual, and web-based materials included.

courses.comments: Course formerly numbered Slavic 4. Russian 4 may be used as a legal repeat of Slavic 4.
courses.description: Focuses on developing fluency, expanding vocabulary, and acquiring basic reading and writing skills. Comprehensive review of basic Russian grammar; introduction to participles and verbal adverbs. Audio, video, and web-based materials are an integral part of the course.

Systematic review of advanced grammar. Compositions, translations, and oral presentations required. Periodic screenings of Russian films.

courses.subject: RUSS
courses.title: The Russian Short Story
courses.prereq_text: Russian 6 or equivalent; and upper-division standing.
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 8 units. Course formerly numbered Slavic 121. Russian 121 may be used as a legal repeat of Slavic 121.
courses.description: Analysis and discussion of various forms of the short story by Russian writers.

courses.subject: RUSS
courses.title: The Russian Novella
courses.prereq_text: Russian 6 or equivalent; and upper-division standing.
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 8 units. Course formerly numbered Slavic 122. Russian 122 may be used as a legal repeat of Slavic 122.
courses.description: In Russian literature the novella is a genre quite distinct from the short story and the novel. All major writers of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries created important works in this form, so that a vast field for exploration and examination exists for such a genre course. Taught in Russian.

courses.subject: RUSS W
courses.title: Advanced Russian
courses.comments: Russian W 101E is the online version of Russian 101E. Russian W 101E may be used as a legal repeat of Russian 101E.
courses.description: This course places an emphasis on communicative ability in contemporary written and spoken Russian and focused study of selected grammatical and stylistic topics. Intensive practice in conversation to develop language skills appropriate to various spheres of academic, business, and social life. Audio-visual materials will be used extensively. By working individually with tutors who are based in Russian-speaking countries, students will augment their speaking skills rapidly.

courses.subject: SLAV
courses.title: Russian Culture
courses.comments: This course is designed for first and second year students.
courses.description: Analyzes crucial trends and issues in Russian culture in their historical, social, and technological settings, from the rise of Moscow in the fifteenth century to post-Soviet Russia. All lectures and readings are in English.

courses.subject: SLAV
courses.title: Short Fiction by Major Russian Writers
courses.description: Survey of short fiction by major Russian short story writers such as Gogol, Dostoevsky, Tolstoy, Chekhov, Bunin, Babel, Nabokov, Petrushevskaya, and Pelevin. Analyzes short story as form and examines works in literary and cultural context. Lectures and readings in English.Designed for first and second year students.

courses.subject: SLAV
courses.title: Great Russian Writers
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 24 units provided letter designations are different, but only 12 units may be applied toward the major.
courses.description: Intensive study of one author. Readings supplemented by select criticism. Readings and lectures in English. Pushkin, Gogol, Leskov, Turgenev, Goncharov, Chekhov, Dostoevsky,Tolstoy, Nabokov, Bulgakov

courses.subject: SLAV
courses.title: Dostoevsky
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 24 units provided letter designations are different, but only 12 units may be applied toward the major.
courses.description: Intensive study of Dostoevsky. Readings supplemented by select criticism. Readings and lectures in English.

courses.subject: SLAV
courses.title: Tolstoy
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 24 units provided letter designations are different, but only 12 units may be applied toward the major.
courses.description: Intensive study of Tolstoy. Readings supplemented by select criticism. Readings and lectures in English.

courses.subject: SLAV
courses.title: Nabokov
courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 24 units provided letter designations are different, but only 12 units may be applied toward the major.
courses.description: Intensive study of Nabokov. Readings supplemented by select criticism. Readings and lectures in English.

courses.subject: SLAV

courses.comments: May be repeated for credit to a maximum of 24 units provided letter designations are different, but only 12 units may be applied toward the major.
courses.description: Intensive study of one writer. Readings supplemented by selected criticism. Taught in English.

courses.subject: SLAV
courses.title: Twentieth-Century Russian Literature I
courses.comments: Not open to credit for students who have completed Slavic 125A.
courses.description: Intensive study of particular authors, genres, literary movements, and selected topics in Russian literature from 1900-1954. Taught in English.

courses.subject: SLAV
courses.title: Twentieth-Century Russian Literature II
